take: Take the memcpy stand-in that states overlap and readable/writable-region checks as __CPROVER_precondition calls before a byte loop, and the generator functions that build a bounded, allocated, valid struct (bounded check, allocate members, assume valid) from nondeterministic fields. They would stand in for hand-built pointer setup and hand-written libc bodies in the harness part of a native case.
why: Native-gate harnesses build arrays and pointers by hand from scalar inputs and use hand-written libc stand-ins; this is a maintained pattern for both.
caveat: The generators call malloc, which dawnr found cannot be used under --cover assume, so they would need an alloca or fixed-array variant; the proof headers include project macros (MAX_ITEM_SIZE) that must be replaced; the memcpy file relies on CBMC private builtins that should be checked against CBMC 6.11.
code_note: memcpy_override.c asserts non-overlap with __CPROVER_POINTER_OBJECT arithmetic and __CPROVER_r_ok/__CPROVER_w_ok on both regions, then copies in a loop, so misuse is reported as a failed precondition instead of an unconstrained havoc. make_common_data_structures.c pairs each *_is_bounded predicate with an ensure_*_has_allocated_* function that mallocs the buffer or leaves it NULL by nondet_bool; failure is a property violation, never a silent return.
falsifier: Replace the hand-written stand-ins and array setup in the existing native cases with these; if the harness text shrinks by fewer than 20 lines per case, or if the native UBSan/ASan replay disagrees with CBMC on any of the cases that were previously cross-checked, it does not help.

take: Lift the way a parser is proven in CBMC: the harness declares only unconstrained pointer and length, while a contracts header names every legal return value as an enum macro and every pre- and postcondition as a predicate, and the Makefile turns on loop contracts and replaces called helpers by their contracts. This gives native_case a way to check loops and callees without a hand-chosen unwind bound.
why: Native loops are bounded by hand and a bound hides defects past it; function and loop contracts remove the bound.
caveat: Contract checking (dfcc, loop contracts) is a CBMC feature set whose stability in 6.11 must be checked on dawnr's cases; the Makefile also selects an external cadical solver, which adds a binary dependency; code is written for CBMC's own build system and would be rewritten as case.json fields.
code_note: core_json_contracts.h defines allocated/old/result as aliases of __CPROVER_is_fresh/__CPROVER_old/__CPROVER_return_value and declares predicate functions such as isValidBuffer and JSON_ValidatePostconditions; the Makefile sets CHECK_FUNCTION_CONTRACTS, APPLY_LOOP_CONTRACTS = 1 and USE_FUNCTION_CONTRACTS for skipCollection/skipSpace. A violated contract surfaces as an ordinary failed CBMC property.
falsifier: Run one existing hand-unwound native case with a loop contract instead of its bound; if CBMC 6.11 does not reach a verdict in 60 seconds on the PX4 wrap_bin control or returns a different verdict than the bounded run, it does not help.

take: Take the table of compiled regular expressions that recognise AddressSanitizer, UBSan, assertion and signal reports, and the crash comparer that decides whether two reports are the same defect. The native replay would use them to classify what the sanitizer build printed and to dedupe witnesses.
why: A CBMC counterexample is only believed after native replay under sanitizers; today the replay judgement is an exit status and a string match, and the finding-to-case cost is the bottleneck.
caveat: constants.py imports clusterfuzz._internal.crash_analysis.stack_parsing, so it cannot be dropped in alone and the regex tables would be copied out; many patterns are Android and Chrome specific and should be pruned; Apache-2.0 notice must travel with a vendored copy.
code_note: constants.py is a flat module of re.compile constants (for example ASAN_DOUBLE_FREE_REGEX, ASAN_MEMCPY_OVERLAP_REGEX, glibc assertion patterns) built to be applied line by line to a log; a line that matches nothing is simply not a frame, so unparsed output degrades to no classification rather than an exception.
falsifier: Feed the sanitizer logs of the 2 replayed PX4 witnesses and the existing synthetic controls through the patterns; if fewer than all of them are assigned the right defect class, or if two distinct witnesses are merged into one, it does not help.

take: Use Sntp_CalculatePollInterval, a function of two uint16 values and an output uint32 pointer whose harness is in the proofs directory, as a ready scalar case source, and the unconstrainedCoreSntpContext allocator in the CBMC state header as the model for building a struct with function-pointer members.
why: Native cases need functions whose inputs are scalars of at most 64 bits; this library has several with a recorded unconstrained-input harness to compare against.
caveat: The harness mallocs its output pointer, which dawnr's gate forbids, so the case must pass the output by address of a local; a library written for embedded targets assumes 32-bit size_t in places.
falsifier: Write the native case for CalculatePollInterval and run the gate; if the original source does not produce a complete verdict on the first attempt or the case takes more than a day of authoring, it does not reduce the finding-to-case cost.

take: The state and network-interface stub headers show how a client that takes caller-supplied function pointers is given nondeterministic transport and time functions, which dawnr could copy for any C target whose parameters include callbacks.
why: Functions that take callbacks or buffers cannot be expressed as scalar inputs, which leaves them without a native case.
caveat: MQTT-specific types; the stubs depend on the library's configuration header; the headers were listed and the README read, not the bodies.
falsifier: Port one callback-taking function from a PX4 or other C source into a case using this stub shape; if more than 2 hand-written stub bodies are still needed, the pattern does not reduce authoring.

take: The AddRangeHeader harness reaches a static function by declaring a wrapper under CBMC's mangled file-local name (__CPROVER_file_local_core_http_client_c_httpHeaderStrncpy) and builds the request-header struct with an allocate helper plus an assumed validity predicate. That is a way to give a static C function a case without editing the extracted source.
why: A native case copies one function unchanged, and many real defects sit in static helpers that a harness cannot name directly.
caveat: The mangled name depends on file name and CBMC version and must be generated per case; the harness uses library types from http_cbmc_state.h that are not read here.
falsifier: Generate the mangled wrapper for 3 static functions in the pinned PX4 or other sources; if CBMC 6.11 does not resolve at least 2 of them, or the verdict differs from an edited non-static copy, it does not help.

take: The CheckOptionsInner harness exercises a byte-stream option reader (prvReadSackOption) with a pointer into a malloc'd buffer of unconstrained size, the usual shape for a function that walks packed bytes. It would be the reference for cases over parsers whose inputs are a buffer plus an index.
why: Arrays and pointers in native cases are built by hand from at-most-64-bit scalars; a buffer-plus-index harness is the missing input shape.
caveat: The harness uses malloc, which cannot be used under --cover assume, and includes FreeRTOS headers; only the buffer-and-index shape transfers.
falsifier: Write one buffer-walking case in this shape for a function with a hand-written loop bound; if the assumption-coverage stage reports more than 1 unreachable goal out of the goals, the shape is not usable under the gate.

take: cbmc_utils.h keeps one nondeterministic index and byte of a buffer (store_byte_from_buffer) before a call and asserts afterwards (assert_blob_equivalence, assert_stuffer_immutable_fields_after_read) that the structure is unchanged, a cheap frame condition that avoids copying the whole buffer.
why: Native cases assert only on return values, so a function that corrupts its input without crashing passes.
caveat: The helpers are typed to s2n_blob and s2n_stuffer and would be rewritten for plain arrays; the file also pulls in OpenSSL reference-count structs that are not needed.
falsifier: Add a not-modified assertion to 3 existing cases using the helper; if no previously clean case turns into a counterexample and no twin gets distinguished, it adds no checking.

take: Build lrat-check.c as a separate checker that reads a DIMACS formula, an LRAT proof and optionally a DRAT file, and prints 'c VERIFIED' only when every hinted clause resolves. Run it on the unsatisfiability proof of the formula a 'complete' native verdict rests on, so that verdict stops depending on trusting the solver.
why: The native gate trusts the SAT solver with no proof certificate, and a 'complete' verdict is an unsatisfiability claim.
caveat: Plain C with a Makefile, built for Linux and macOS; on Windows it would run under MSYS or WSL. Some error paths (a comment longer than 1024 characters, usage) call exit(0), so the result must be taken from the printed line, not the exit status. Memory use grows with the proof, and CBMC must be made to emit a DIMACS formula and the solver an LRAT proof for the same encoding.
code_note: lrat-check.c keeps a hash table of live clauses by id; for each proof line it checks that no hint refers to a deleted clause and that unit propagation over the hints reaches a conflict. Failures print 'c ERROR: using DELETED hint clause', 'c FAILED: tautology' or 'c failed while checking clause: ...' and return FAILED; only a full pass prints 'c VERIFIED'.
falsifier: Produce a proof for the PX4 wrap_bin fixed-variant formula and check it; if the proof cannot be generated and checked within 30 minutes and 8 GB on the 16 GB laptop, or if a deliberately corrupted proof line is not rejected, it does not help.

take: Use CaDiCaL as the SAT back end for the exported native formula with its LRAT tracer switched on, and its built-in LratChecker class to check each derived clause as it is learned. This gives dawnr both a proof file and an in-process check of one solver run.
why: A complete native verdict is a SAT-unsatisfiable claim with no certificate, and the formula can be solved a second time by a solver with a different design.
caveat: C++ solver built with its configure script, so Windows needs MSYS or WSL; CBMC's own SAT back end must be bypassed by exporting a formula, which loses CBMC's incremental queries; checker failure aborts the solver process, so the harness must run it as a subprocess.
code_note: LratChecker is a Tracer: it stores clauses in a hash table keyed by id, marks literals during unit propagation and verifies each resolution chain (check_resolution). On a bad chain it calls fatal_message_start() and aborts the process, so a wrong proof cannot pass silently.
falsifier: Solve the exported formula for the PX4 original and fixed variants with LRAT on; if solving takes more than twice the time CBMC's own solver took on the same case or the produced proof is rejected by drat-trim's lrat-check, it does not help.

take: Second checker for the same proofs: its README says it does not ignore unit-clause deletions by default and, after rejecting a proof, writes a SICK certificate of incorrectness that rate-sick-check can validate. Using it beside drat-trim gives two independently written checkers of one proof.
why: Agreement between front ends sharing code is not independence; two proof checkers written separately are cheap to compare.
caveat: Rust crate (cargo build, last pushed 2022-02), so it needs a Rust toolchain on the build machine; the README says it is faster than drat-trim and DPR checking is also supported; not read beyond README and tree.
falsifier: Run both checkers over 20 proofs including 5 corrupted ones; if they ever disagree on a proof's validity and the disagreement is not a documented unit-deletion difference, the pair adds nothing.

take: Kissat is a second, differently designed solver to run on the exported native formula, and its src directory lists proof.c, check.c and resolve.c for proof output and checking (file names only, bodies not read). A SAT or UNSAT answer that both Kissat and CaDiCaL give for one formula is cross-solver agreement.
why: The SAT solver is trusted alone today; solver diversity is the cheapest second opinion.
caveat: C solver that builds on Linux and macOS; a Windows build is not documented in the files read; README and tree only.
falsifier: Run it against CaDiCaL on all native formulas; if the two ever disagree on SAT or UNSAT, or Kissat is more than 5 times slower on the largest formula, it is not a usable second solver.
code_note: proof.c holds kissat_init_proof(solver, file, binary), which selects binary or textual proof tracing and logs which, write helpers that import internal and external literals, and a flush_buffer that calls kissat_fatal when writing the buffered proof fails, so a short write aborts the solver instead of leaving a silently truncated proof.

take: PySAT gives Python access to several SAT solvers, a CNF formula class and cardinality encodings from one pip install. It would let a dawnr script re-solve a native formula with different solvers and assemble extra constraints without shelling out.
why: Native gate needs a second solver and a place to run checks from Python 3.12; pysat wraps several.
caveat: Needs a C compiler or prebuilt wheels per platform; Python 3.12 or later wheel availability must be checked; most of its solvers are older than Kissat and CaDiCaL.
falsifier: Re-solve the native formulas with two PySAT solvers; if any disagrees with the gate's verdict or install fails on one of the 3 platforms, it does not help.

take: Study how a Python driver splits a large C source file into one function at a time with a small state machine (name and parameter extraction, comment skipping, brace counting) and verifies each function with ESBMC. It is a lighter route than libclang to the per-function extraction step of a native case.
why: Each native case needs the function body extracted unchanged from a pinned source; automating extraction cuts the finding-to-case cost.
caveat: The function splitter is regular-expression based (it expects return type, name and parameters on one line and strips block comments line by line), so it fails on macros, K&R definitions and multi-line signatures; ESBMC rather than CBMC; the repository ships its own esbmc binary under lsverifier/bin, which dawnr would not use.
code_note: parse_functions reads the file line by line in states GET_NAME_AND_PARAMS, BLOCK_COMMENT and GET_BODY, counting open braces to find the end of a body; a line it cannot match is silently skipped rather than raising, so malformed input yields fewer functions instead of an error.
falsifier: Run its splitter over the pinned PX4 and 4 other C sources already used as cases; if it recovers fewer than 90 percent of function definitions that native_case's one-function range check accepts, it does not help.

take: Its README describes an SMT solver library with work-in-progress proof generation, and the proof-trace-dump.sh script dumps traces. It is a reading source for how a proof trace of an SMT query is structured before any such certificate is attempted for CBMC's bit-vector queries.
why: SMT answers in the native and Z3-using paths also have no certificate.
caveat: OCaml library; proof generation is described as work in progress; no direct path from CBMC to this solver.
falsifier: Express one native bit-vector query in SMT-LIB and ask for a proof; if no checkable proof comes back for 3 of 3 queries, drop it.

take: Lift the voluptuous schemas that validate CBMC's JSON loop map, coverage and trace output before use, and the Status enum that raises on an unknown coverage status. They harden native_check's reading of CBMC output so that a changed field cannot be read as a pass.
why: A harness that returns early or a goal CBMC reports in a new form must not become a 'complete' verdict; the gate's own reader should refuse unknown shapes.
caveat: The package imports voluptuous and its own helper modules (runt, srcloct, util), so single files cannot be copied alone; whether its parsers accept plain cbmc --json-ui output was not checked.
code_note: loopt.py defines VALID_LOOP as a voluptuous Schema (loop name to source location), merges loop maps and logs a warning on duplicate definitions instead of overwriting silently; coveraget.py raises UserWarning on an unknown line-coverage status and tracks an incomplete-coverage flag.
falsifier: Feed the existing CBMC 6.11 outputs of all native controls (36 pilot tests) through the schemas; if any valid output is rejected, or a hand-edited output with a renamed property field is still accepted, it does not help.

take: Lift the harness vocabulary of DeepState: typed symbolic draws, DeepState_Assume with the expression text recorded, ranged draws that assume low <= x <= high, and a concretize call, written once and run against several engines. A native case could then be one source file that CBMC, a fuzzer and the ASan replay all execute.
why: Native cases generate the CBMC harness and a separate native replay from the same description; one harness vocabulary would remove the second translation.
caveat: Last push 2025-08 and its symbolic back ends (Manticore, angr) differ from CBMC; a CBMC back end would have to be written; headers are C and C++ and there is a Win32 source beside the UNIX one.
code_note: DeepState.h declares DeepState_Assume(x) as a macro that passes the expression string, file and line, plus DeepState_Abandon and DeepState_Fail and IsSymbolic predicates per integer width; a failed assume abandons the test rather than reporting a failure.
falsifier: Re-express the PX4 wrap_bin case as a DeepState-style source and replay it; if the CBMC witness cannot be replayed with the same inputs through this vocabulary, or the translation needs more lines than native_case.py's own replay, it does not help.

take: The repository holds the witness exchange format (GraphML and YAML), a JSON schema for loop-invariant witnesses, a lint directory with faulty-witness examples and a test-harnesses directory. The faulty examples give negative controls for any dawnr reader of CBMC or CPAchecker witnesses.
why: Counterexamples are replayed natively but never validated in the SV-COMP witness format, so a witness from another tool cannot be compared.
caveat: Archived with a note that the project moved; the format has since been revised, so the current specification must be fetched before use; README-level reading plus listing of lint and test-harnesses.
falsifier: Run the 3 faulty examples through a reader built on the schema; if any is accepted, the lint helps nothing.

take: CPAchecker is a second verifier to run on C sources beside CBMC: the config directory lists a k-induction configuration (bmc-induction), incremental BMC and a correctness-witness validation configuration. Disagreement between CPAchecker and CBMC on one case is independent evidence the pilot lacks.
why: One engine decides every native verdict; the pilot has no second tool and no k-induction to remove hand-set loop bounds.
caveat: Java application needing a JRE; its C front end differs from GCC and ILP32 or LP64 handling must be set per run; it is a read-only mirror of an upstream repository; only the config names and the README were read.
falsifier: Run bmc-induction on 5 cases whose CBMC loops are hand-bounded; if it proves none of them or contradicts a CBMC verdict on a control, it does not help.

take: UTopia derives fuzz drivers from a library's existing unit tests; its README says it supports C and C++ libraries. Turning an existing unit test into a harness is a way to get a harness body, with realistic argument setup, without writing one.
why: Every native harness is hand-written; deriving them from tests already in the project removes the authoring step and also covers C++.
caveat: Ships a docker directory and git submodules (external/); last push 2025-04; output targets libFuzzer rather than CBMC, so only the extraction logic transfers.
falsifier: Run it over a library with unit tests and count how many generated drivers compile; if fewer than half do or none can be adapted to a scalar-input case, it does not help.

take: PromeFuzz assembles a model prompt from structured code metadata, documentation and API knowledge to write C and C++ fuzzing harnesses, and its processor directory (judging by its name, not read) is where the metadata extraction would sit. dawnr could reuse the prompt inputs for a native harness drafter whose output the existing CBMC gate then judges.
why: The finding-to-case cost is dominated by hand-written harnesses; a drafter whose output is checked by the gate cannot make a false verdict.
caveat: Requires an external model, with a Dockerfile and setup script in the tree; the harness type is libFuzzer, not CBMC; this entry is README and tree only.
falsifier: Draft harnesses for 10 functions and run them through the gate; if fewer than 3 reach a complete or counterexample verdict without hand edits, drafting does not lower the cost.

take: CKGFuzzer builds a code knowledge graph of API usage and feeds it to a model that writes fuzz drivers; a fuzzing_llm_engine directory is listed (not read). It is a reading source for choosing which callers and call sequences to show a model drafting a harness.
why: A harness for a function with pointer arguments needs to know how callers build them.
caveat: Speculative for dawnr's scalar cases; depends on an LLM and a Docker environment; not read beyond README and tree.
falsifier: Show the graph's caller snippets to a model drafting 5 pointer-argument harnesses; if the number of harnesses that compile does not exceed the number without snippets, drop it.

take: libErator generates fuzz drivers from library source without consumer code, and a condition_extractor directory is listed, which by its name (not read) extracts argument conditions. Such conditions are the same information needed for the assumptions of a native harness.
why: Assumption statements in native harnesses are written by hand from reading the source.
caveat: Artifact repository for a paper with a large LLVM build, custom libFuzzer and Docker; heavy for any direct use; paths read from the tree only.
falsifier: Extract conditions for 5 functions whose hand harness assumptions are known; if fewer than 3 of 5 recover the assumptions already written, it does not help.

take: UTBot C/C++ generates test cases that try to cover statements and paths and treats the source as the truth for a regression suite; its server directory (judging by its name, not read) is where the generator would sit. For a C++ function with no native case, generated tests with concrete inputs would give seeds for a harness.
why: A C++ function has no native case at all.
caveat: Last push 2024-10; the tree has docker, submodules and editor plugins; produces regression tests that assume the current behaviour is correct, so it does not find the specification.
falsifier: Generate tests for one C++ function from PX4 and replay them under UBSan; if none exercises a boundary value the existing C cases did, it does not help.

take: DARPA Challenge Binaries ported to Linux, macOS and Windows: the README calls them programs designed to contain vulnerabilities, and each challenge directory sits beside a pov directory. They are a corpus of C functions with planted, documented defects to test whether the native gate finds a known bug.
why: The gate has found few real bugs; a corpus with known defects measures its recall.
caveat: Last push 2023-06; many challenges are whole programs with their own libc shim rather than scalar-input functions, so function extraction is manual.
falsifier: Write native cases for 10 challenge functions with a known defect; if the gate finds fewer than 5 of 10, recall is below 50 percent and the corpus has told us so.

take: GenMC is a stateless model checker for concurrent C, C++ and Rust at the LLVM IR level; it is the only engine in this list built for concurrent C functions.
why: Concurrent functions in the flight code have no model-checked case; the gate has no thread model.
caveat: Needs LLVM and a C++ toolchain; a mirror of an internal repository updated periodically; concurrency is outside what native_case.py states today. Per its README it is available as a Docker image (genmc/genmc) or built from source with a C++20 compiler and an LLVM installation (versions 19 and 20 listed), so a native Windows build is not offered.
falsifier: Model one PX4 lock-protected update with it; if no property is checkable without rewriting the code, drop it.

take: TriCera is a model checker for C programs from Uppsala that accepts structs, arrays and heap operations and has an ACSL parser. It can serve as a third verifier on the same case descriptions and its regression-tests directory shows C programs with contract annotations. Its README says it encodes the program into Constrained Horn Clauses, supports function contracts, structs, arrays and heap operations (malloc, calloc, free) but not pointer arithmetic, and ships example .c files under regression-tests.
why: Heap and array programs are where the gate's hand-built inputs are weakest.
caveat: Scala and sbt project; pointer arithmetic is not supported according to its README; platform support was not checked.
falsifier: Run 5 array cases through it; if it produces a verdict on fewer than 3 or contradicts CBMC on a control, drop it.

take: Haybale is a symbolic execution engine for LLVM IR written in Rust; it also has a tests directory. It is a source for ideas about producing concrete inputs for a path, the step before a native replay. Its README compares it to KLEE and says it reasons about all possible inputs to a function without brute force.
why: Native replay needs concrete inputs from a witness; a path-oriented engine produces them without a SAT trace.
caveat: Last push 2023-10; Rust crate that needs an LLVM version matching the one that compiles the target.
falsifier: Ask it for an input that reaches the wrap_bin assertion; if it returns none that CBMC's witness set contains, drop it.

take: Run Mariposa's idea on the SMT queries the seven lowerings send to Z3 and cvc5: create semantics-preserving mutants of each query, solve them, and let a proportions z-test (statsmodels) assign a stability category of stable, unstable, unsolvable or unknown. A proof that passes only on one query ordering becomes a labelled result instead of a pass.
why: Proof results can be unstable and the SPARK relu_all twin exhausts its budget; the repository measures that instability per query instead of by anecdote.
caveat: Python with a Rust helper (src/smt2action) that must be built with cargo; the repository ships many Z3 and cvc5 solver binaries under bin/, which are not MIT code and should not be redistributed; experiment hosts are hard-coded in src/base/defs.py (a cluster), so only the analysis and mutation code are meant; it operates on SMT-LIB queries, so it covers only the kernels that send queries to an SMT solver.
code_note: query_analyzer.py defines Stability (STABLE, UNSTABLE, UNSOLVABLE, UNKNOWN) and FailureType enums, classifies a group of mutant runs against a timeout cutoff in _categorize_cutoff or by a strict mode, and imports proportions_ztest to decide whether a fraction of successes differs from the original; an unsolvable group is a separate category from an unstable one.
falsifier: Collect the SMT queries for the 7 twins' obligations from Dafny and Verus and mutate each 10 times; if the share classified unstable is under 5 percent, or the unstable ones do not include the SPARK relu_all budget case, it explains nothing about dawnr's instability.

take: Lift the round-trip check: a model reads only the formal lemma and writes it back as plain English without seeing the requirement, and a second call compares that English with the requirement, with both calls forced into JSON tool schemas. For dawnr this is a test of whether a verified t specification says what its natural-language problem asked.
why: Gate precision is 0.682 against a required 0.70 and a clean answer has been shown to disagree with its own problem; this checks meaning, not strength.
caveat: Node.js code that calls Claude models through API, Bedrock, Vertex or Claude Code, so its prompts must be ported to Cohere or a local model for use and none of its model-written evaluation outputs may be training data; its examples are Dafny lemmas, not t.
code_note: roundtrip.js picks a backend, resolves a model tier name to an id, calls the informalize tool and then the compare tool with schemas from schemas.js, and throws on an unsupported option combination; the comparison result is returned beside the intermediate English so a person can read both.
falsifier: Run the round trip on the 1,038 proved training answers with a local model; if its disagreement flags miss the 1 exploitable specification among the 11 clean answers, or flag more than 30 percent of the 1,038 proved answers, it does not help.

take: Each directory under projects holds a Dockerfile, build.sh and project.yaml for an enrolled open-source project with a fuzz target (for example bzip2 and boost-json), and the seeded-projects table lists them. These are ready-made pairs of real C and C++ code and a harness entry point to mine for native cases.
why: Finding real defects costs most at the step from a located function to a harness; these projects already name the entry point and how to build it.
caveat: The README says the program proves theorems about compiled fuzz targets; the project directories are build recipes and the sources are fetched at build time; a Docker dependency; the proofs themselves are in a separate repository.
falsifier: Pick 10 fuzz targets from the table and derive a scalar-input native case from each; if fewer than 3 yield a function with inputs of at most 64 bits, the list is not a case source.

take: Plausible is a property-testing framework inside Lean 4 tactics that reports a counterexample with shrinking, shown in its README on a false array statement. Running it on the Lean lowering's goals before a proof attempt gives a counterexample witness for cheap and a pre-filter for wrong specifications.
why: Lean is one of seven kernels and its failures give no witness; a counterexample first would also feed the witness-fed repair round.
caveat: Lean 4 package pinned by lean-toolchain; works on goals whose types have Sampleable and Shrinkable instances, so t's value kinds need instances; README and file names only.
falsifier: Run it on the Lean lowering of the 213 broken twins with numInst 100; if it reports failure with a counterexample for fewer than half, or reports success on any broken twin, it is not a usable witness source.
code_note: Testable.lean defines TestResult with three cases: success (optionally with a proof), gaveUp n (n invalid examples were tried) and failure carrying a proof that the property does not hold plus the counterexample strings and the number of shrinks; the configuration has numInst (default 100) and maxSize (default 100), so a run that cannot find valid examples reports gaveUp rather than a pass.

take: Lemmafit puts a Dafny verifier into an agent's edit loop: its README describes business logic and state machines proved in Dafny and the code generated from them, and cli and skills hold the loop. It is a reading source for how verifier output is returned to a model in the coding-agent setting. Its README says business logic is written in Dafny, verified and compiled to TypeScript, installed with npm, and driven through Claude Code, which makes the loop's model a commercial one.
why: One round of witness-fed repair moved few cells; how an agent product returns verifier messages is a data point about the missing ingredient.
caveat: Node.js and Claude Code skills; no Dafny-specific repair algorithm inspected; kept as C.
falsifier: Replay its message format for 20 failing Dafny cells in one repair round; if the cells repaired do not exceed the plain-message baseline of the same round, drop it.

take: Goose translates a subset of Go to Rocq with a semantics in Coq; its proofgen and glang directories generate and define the target. It is an example of a translator whose output is proved to preserve meaning by being a model in the proof assistant, which is the translation-validation question for dawnr's lowerings. Its README says the translator and semantics are trusted and the semantics is given by translation to an untyped lambda calculus with references and concurrency.
why: No lowering of t to a proof system has a check that the lowered program means the same as the source.
caveat: The repository is archived and says development moved to Perennial; Go and Coq stack unrelated to t.
falsifier: Express the interpreter semantics of 3 t programs in the Rocq lowering via this style; if the generated model fails to match the Python interpreter on any of 20 inputs, it does not give validation.

take: RacerF and DeadlockF are Frama-C plugins (compatible with Frama-C 29.0 per the README) that detect data races and deadlocks using a plugin API that dawnr's Frama-C lowering does not use. They show how to write a Frama-C plugin in OCaml with dune, if the lowering ever needs analysis beyond WP.
why: Frama-C once emitted an invariant of its own that was false; plugin-level checks of emitted code are a possible guard.
caveat: OCaml and opam; plugin API tracks Frama-C versions closely.
falsifier: Port a trivial plugin that lists emitted invariants; if the plugin cannot be built against the Frama-C version dawnr pins, drop it.

take: The SAW and Coq directories hold specifications and proof scripts for AWS libcrypto written in two different proof systems over the same C, with Cryptol reference specifications in a submodule. It is a worked case of one C function verified by two independent tool chains, the setup that dawnr's seven-way gate imitates.
why: Agreement between front ends sharing solvers is not independence; this project's two chains (SAW with SMT, Coq) are a real example of what independence costs.
caveat: Needs SAW, Cryptol, Docker images per architecture; specifications are crypto-specific; the README says recent work moved to s2n-bignum, so some directories may be historical.
falsifier: Count how many of the verified functions have proofs in both chains; if fewer than 5, it is no example of redundant verification.

take: Vendor the Muon optimizer class from the first Muon record: SGD with Nesterov momentum followed by a five-step Newton-Schulz orthogonalisation of each 2-D update, run in bfloat16. It would be the optimizer arm of a locallm run for weight matrices, with Adam kept for embeddings and norms.
why: The locallm model computed the right function about once on 200 unseen problems; the optimizer is a cheap, separable variable and the repository records its effect on a small model's loss.
caveat: The speedrun's current files target 8 H100 GPUs with fp8 and CUDA graphs, so only the early single-file record is taken; Muon should be applied to 2-D hidden matrices only; the claim of speed is the repository's, on FineWeb, not on t.
code_note: zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 normalises the gradient by its norm and iterates a quintic polynomial in bfloat16, with an SVD backend kept for comparison; the Muon class keeps a momentum buffer per parameter in its state and applies the orthogonalised step, so a shape that is not 2-D is the caller's responsibility rather than a checked error.
falsifier: Train the current locallm size twice on the same token budget, one with Muon and one with the current optimizer; if validation loss on the held-out split is not lower by 0.02 nats, or the number of correct functions on the 200 unseen problems does not rise above 1, it does not help.

take: Read the 64M-parameter pretraining loop for its resume handling (SkipBatchSampler and an optimizer, scaler and step checkpoint) and the converter that exports the trained model to a transformers layout. That converter is the step before llama.cpp conversion to GGUF for the local model.
why: Training budget is limited and one RTX 4080 is the local card; a resumable single-GPU loop and an export path to a standard layout are required for any short run to be continued.
caveat: Most README text and comments are Chinese; the model layout is MiniMind's own, so the converter maps to a Llama or Qwen-style class only for compatible shapes; the pretraining recipe's data is not a code corpus.
code_note: train_pretrain.py scales the learning rate per step with a schedule function, divides the loss by the accumulation steps, clips gradients, and saves checkpoint, optimizer, scaler, epoch and step so --from_resume 1 can continue; convert_model.py has separate functions for torch to transformers and back, and for merging a LoRA into the base weights.
falsifier: Export a locallm checkpoint through a ported converter and compare held-out perplexity in PyTorch and in llama.cpp; if the two differ by more than 1 percent, or a resumed run's loss at the resume step differs from the uninterrupted run, it does not help.

take: Lift the learning-rate schedule functions for a constant-then-cool-down (wsd_schedule with linear, cosine and exponential decay types) and the weight-averaging code from the paper's codebase. A short cool-down on a trained checkpoint is a way to get a better final model without fixing the total steps in advance.
why: Training budget is limited, and continuing a run from a checkpoint (as the r12 runs do) needs a schedule that does not assume a fixed length.
caveat: Based on nanoGPT-style loops and OpenWebText-scale data; the paper's claim is for language-model loss on web text and says nothing about t; module imports its own config objects.
code_note: wsd_schedule returns a function of the step with a warmup, a constant phase and a decay whose type is chosen by name; an unknown decay type raises a ValueError listing the allowed names, so a typo cannot silently fall back to a default.
falsifier: Continue the last locallm checkpoint with a 10 percent cool-down and compare to continuing with the existing schedule; if held-out validation loss does not improve by 0.01 nats, or the 32 contaminated problems are the only ones that gain, it does not help.

take: LLM.Q trains with fp8 and other quantised weights and gradients in C++ and CUDA, and its README gives timings for Qwen2.5-0.5B on RTX 4090 cards and an export-checkpoint tool. The numbers and the recipes show what a single Ada-generation card can train, which is the RTX 4080's architecture.
why: One RTX 4080 is the only local card; quantised training decides whether a larger code model fits it.
caveat: C++20 and CUDA 12 build with nccl and cudnn dependencies; the README lists RTX 4090 and RTX PRO 6000 runs, not a 4080 (16 GB), so memory fit is untested; Linux build.
falsifier: Run its 0.5B recipe on the 4080; if peak memory exceeds 16 GB or tokens per second is below half of the PyTorch bf16 baseline, it does not help.

take: Meta Lingua is a small PyTorch training library whose README describes the checkpoint, data-loader and distributed modules separately and shows a one-GPU launch. Its checkpoint module and data loader are a compact reference for a resumable loader whose exactness would have to be tested.
why: Locallm continues runs from checkpoints; resuming must not repeat or skip tokens.
caveat: README says data preparation uses terashuf and downloads fineweb_edu; the library targets multi-GPU clusters, so only the single-device path is relevant.
falsifier: Compare resumed-run token order with the existing loader after a kill at step 100; if any batch differs, the loader pattern is not exact.

take: OLMo-core packages the building blocks of the OLMo training stack as a PyTorch library, with the data, optimizer and checkpoint pieces separated into modules under src/olmo_core. It is a reading reference for how a fully open pretraining stack organises its pieces. Its README says it installs by pip as ai2-olmo-core after PyTorch and has optional dependencies such as flash-attn and TransformerEngine.
why: Locallm's trainer grew experiment by experiment; a documented module layout is a comparison point.
caveat: Built for large multi-node runs; dependency heavy; only the layout is of use.
falsifier: List which of its modules locallm lacks; if none changes a measured result, the layout is only reading.

take: EasyDistill composes generation, evaluation, filtering, rewriting, balancing and preference-scoring operators from a config into a pipeline that outputs SFT and DPO data from a teacher model. The operator list and config schema are a model for dawnr's teacher recipes.
why: Cohere teacher runs added zero rows; a pipeline with an explicit filter and balance stage names where rows are lost.
caveat: Intended for black-box teachers behind an API, including models whose output dawnr must not train on; only the pipeline structure is taken, never its data.
falsifier: Re-express one existing teacher recipe as such a pipeline and count rows at each stage; if no stage has a count that the current logs lack, it adds nothing.

take: AutoRound is a post-training quantisation toolkit whose README lists GGUF among its export formats (added July 2025), with an AutoScheme for accuracy at low bit widths. It could produce the quantised GGUF of the local model with a calibration set drawn from t programs.
why: dawnr ask takes 64.6 s from a cold start and 6.8 GB peak; a smaller quantisation is a direct lever on both.
caveat: Targets Hugging Face transformers models, so a locallm checkpoint must first be in that layout; calibration on t text is untested; the listed path is the package directory.
falsifier: Quantise the current checkpoint to 4 bits with a t calibration set; if the clean count on the 232 held-out problems drops by more than 1 answer or peak memory stays above 5 GB, it does not help.

take: Lift the mask-store construction: for each lexer terminal and automaton state it precomputes the set of vocabulary tokens that can follow, caches the table on disk, and at decode time looks up the allowed tokens from the parser's accepted terminal sequences. It would give locallm a grammar mask for t built on an LR parser, not a fresh regular-expression filter.
why: The syntax gate loses more model answers than every other gate together, tolerant readers rescue little and the fix has to be at generation.
caveat: Its README says Python 3.13 is not supported and dawnr requires 3.12 or later, so the interpreter must be 3.12; it carries its own copy of Lark code under syncode/larkm; the cache is stored with pickle, which must not be loaded from an untrusted path; masks are torch tensors over a Hugging Face tokenizer vocabulary, so a llama.cpp path needs separate work.
code_note: MaskStore.init_mask_store tries to pickle.load a cached store and on any exception rebuilds it and pickle.dump's it, so a corrupt cache is rebuilt rather than failing; _store_token_masks builds the per-terminal token masks, _lookup_next_tokens raises ValueError on an invalid accept sequence, and is_valid_prefix returns a boolean for a partial parse.
falsifier: Decode the 232 held-out problems with the t grammar through this mask on the same model; if the parse-failure count does not fall by at least 50 percent from the unconstrained run, or tests passed do not exceed the earlier constrained result of 1.23 times, it does not help.

take: Formatron builds format constraints from pydantic models, JSON schemas and regular expressions and, per its README, runs an Earley parser implemented in Rust with caching across generations, with transformers, vllm, exllamav2 and RWKV integrations. Its schema classes are the model for generating a constraint from a problem's signature.
why: The next teacher-data step builds schemas from the problem's signature that restrict types and in-scope names; this library already turns typed schemas into token constraints.
caveat: Its README has a feature table that includes llama.cpp and says a technical report exists; Rust extension for the Earley engine means a wheel must exist for each platform; code not read beyond file names.
falsifier: Express a signature-derived schema for 20 problems and decode them; if more than 2 of 20 schemas cannot be represented, the pattern cannot carry the type and scope restriction, and if tokens per second falls below half of unconstrained decoding it is too slow.
code_note: formatter.py defines FormatterBase with accept_token, accept_bytes, compute_allowed_tokens, mask_logits, is_completed and captures, and a Formatter that holds a kbnf.Engine and returns kbnf's AcceptTokenResult from try_accept_new_token, so a token the grammar rejects is reported by value, not by exception; the grammar string is exposed for inspection.

take: This code constrains diffusion language models with context-free grammars and ships a Rust formal-language library (rustformlang) with bindings and examples for JSON Schema, C++ and SMILES. The formal-language library, intersecting a grammar with a regular constraint, is reusable for any decoder that can fill in masked spans.
why: Fill-in-the-middle is how locallm fills holes in a spec; a grammar-aware fill needs the intersection operations this library implements.
caveat: Rust toolchain required for rustformlang bindings; written for diffusion models; README-level reading only.
falsifier: Use the intersection to enumerate completions of 50 holes in t programs; if more than 5 percent of valid t completions are excluded, the grammar is too strict.

take: treereduce shrinks source code with tree-sitter grammars while preserving a property such as a compiler crash or an output message. It could reduce a bug-triggering C function to the part the native case needs.
why: The finding-to-case cost is the bottleneck: real bugs sit in functions much larger than the harness needs.
caveat: Rust binary built with cargo; it needs a script that tests the property to preserve, which here would run the native gate; reduces syntax, not meaning, so the reduced function may no longer be the original defect.
falsifier: Reduce 5 functions whose native case already exists; if the reduced function loses the CBMC counterexample in more than 1 of 5, it is not a safe step.

take: A Python library for building llama.cpp GBNF grammars from a rule object model; its compiler turns the objects into grammar text. It shows how to build a grammar for the local model programmatically instead of writing text by hand.
why: The local model is run through llama.cpp, whose only constraint mechanism is a grammar; t's grammar needs to be written in GBNF.
caveat: Last push 2023-11; tiny; code not read.
falsifier: Compile t's grammar and test it with llama.cpp on the 232 problems; if more than 0 well-formed answers are rejected, the grammar is wrong.

take: Python-SPARK is an Earley-algorithm parser toolkit in pure Python with generic AST routines; spark_parser holds the implementation. It is a small, dependency-free place to read Earley prediction, scanning and completion before writing a prefix-validity check for t.
why: Earley prefix automata are named in the constrained-generation part of the project and a plain-Python reference lowers the cost of building one.
caveat: Older code base; not designed for incremental prefixes; Python 3.12 compatibility untested.
falsifier: Port a prefix-validity test on top of it; if it takes more than 10 ms per prefix on the longest t program, it is too slow for a decoding loop.

take: A harness that runs several structured-output frameworks on the same tasks and reports failures and latency from a config file. Its frameworks directory shows how to compare frameworks under one interface.
why: Choosing among constraint backends needs the same comparison on the same inputs.
caveat: Last push 2024-09; tasks are classification and NER, not code; API-based frameworks.
falsifier: Wrap xgrammar and SynCode in its interface; if the comparison cannot report parse failures per backend, it does not help.

take: Lift the run loop of DefaultAgent: a model reply that does not parse raises FormatError, the error text goes back to the model as the next message, a counter of consecutive format errors ends the run with a named exit status, and the transcript is saved after every step in a finally block. dawnr_agent's loop could use the same ending conditions and per-step journal.
why: A small local model's malformed replies are the main loss in the assistant path; the loop needs a bounded, recorded response to them rather than a crash or an endless retry.
caveat: Needs pydantic and its own model and environment interfaces; the loop assumes a chat model that can follow a single-command format, which the local model has not been measured on; the repository also supports Docker and Singularity environments that are not needed.
code_note: run() resets n_consecutive_format_errors after any clean step, adds the failed call's cost before counting the error, appends an exit message with status RepeatedFormatError once the configured maximum is reached, passes InterruptAgentFlow messages through, logs and re-raises any other exception, and always calls save().
falsifier: Replay 50 recorded locallm assistant sessions through this loop shape; if the share of sessions ending in an unrecorded crash is not zero, or the share reaching a final answer does not rise above the current rate, it does not help.

take: Study how it builds the command line for bubblewrap on Linux (unshare, read-only binds, mandatory deny paths) and the sandbox-exec profile on macOS around an arbitrary process, with proxy-filtered network. dawnr could apply the same recipes to the processes that run model-written code and builds.
why: The repository assistant runs shell commands and sandboxed builds on Linux and macOS laptops; a tested recipe for OS-level restriction is cheaper than writing one.
caveat: TypeScript on Node, with a Rust toolchain file and vendor directory; its README names only sandbox-exec on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux, so Windows, one of dawnr's three platforms, needs a different mechanism; only the policy recipes are meant to be ported.
code_note: linux-sandbox-utils.ts documents bwrap behaviours it works around (for example that --ro-bind /dev/null onto a symlink makes bwrap abort at startup), computes mandatory deny paths for the working directory, and checks bounding capabilities from /proc status before choosing a seccomp helper.
falsifier: Run 20 model-written shell commands that try to read outside the repository and write to the home directory under a ported policy; if any one succeeds, or legitimate build commands fail more than 2 times in 20, it does not help.

take: Take the edit tool that applies a line-range replacement, runs a linter on the result, and refuses the edit when it introduces new syntax errors, returning both the would-be window and the original with an instruction not to repeat the command. It is an edit format whose failure mode is a message instead of a corrupted file.
why: A small local model writing edits produces invalid code often; rejecting an edit that adds a syntax error keeps the working tree usable and the error text feeds the next attempt.
caveat: Uses a flake8 helper for Python only; other languages need their own checker; imports from the repository's windowed and registry libraries, so the script is lifted as a pattern, not run as is.
code_note: The script parses a start:end range and replacement from stdin, builds a WindowedFile, applies the edit, runs flake8 on the file before and after, and on new errors undoes the edit, prints _LINT_ERROR_TEMPLATE with the errors and both windows and exits 1; usage errors print a usage message.
falsifier: Run 100 model edits to Python files with and without the lint gate; if the number of files left with a syntax error after the session is not lower by at least 10, or successful edits fall by more than 5, it does not help.

take: BM25S implements BM25 in Python on NumPy, with separate scoring, tokenization and selection modules and a numba directory for an optional compiled path. It could replace or cross-check the BM25 ranking in the local retrieval package.
why: dawnr ask takes 64.6 s from a cold start; how much of that is retrieval index build was not measured here, and this is one component that can be swapped and timed.
caveat: Pure Python wheels, NumPy required, Numba optional (Numba support for Python 3.13 must be checked); tokenizer is word-based and not code aware, so identifiers need splitting before use.
falsifier: Index the repository corpus used by the retrieval recall test and compare recall at 10 and index build time with the present BM25; if recall drops by more than 1 point or build time is not at least halved, it does not help.
code_note: scoring.py builds document frequencies, an idf array and a non-occurrence array for the BM25L and BM25+ variants with k1 and b parameters; numba is imported optionally and a dummy decorator is defined when it is missing, so the code runs without numba, only slower.

take: sqlite-vec is a vector-search extension for SQLite written as a single C file with bindings and benchmark scripts, so embeddings could be stored next to chunk text in the same database file without a separate vector service.
why: Memory peak of 6.8 GB on a laptop during dawnr ask matters; a vector store inside SQLite avoids loading a separate index process.
caveat: Loading a SQLite extension needs a compatible build of Python's sqlite3 per platform (not checked on all three platforms); the tree has two licence files, LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT, and the platform reports Apache-2.0.
falsifier: Store the corpus embeddings and compare query latency and peak memory with the current dense index; if peak memory is not lower or recall at 10 differs by more than 1 point, it does not help.

take: grep-ast shows lines matching a pattern together with the enclosing loops, functions and classes found by tree-sitter, so a retrieval result arrives with the context a person needs to read it.
why: Context management for a small model needs matched lines with their enclosing definition, not whole files.
caveat: Depends on tree-sitter language packs, which are native wheels per platform; last push 2025-05; small project, so output format is the only part that is certain.
falsifier: Replace line-window context with enclosing-definition context for 50 retrieval queries; if answer correctness on the repository question set does not rise by 2 answers of 50, drop it.

take: ast-grep is a Rust command-line tool that matches code by syntax tree patterns and rewrites matches, with a JSON schema for its rule files. A model could be given pattern rewrites as an edit format that is structurally valid, rather than line ranges.
why: Line-range edits break on indentation and drift; a structural edit names what it changes.
caveat: Rust binary distributed through npm and pip; the model must learn the pattern syntax, which a small model may not write correctly.
falsifier: Offer structural rewrites for 30 edit tasks and compare success with line-range edits; if success is below the line-range rate, drop it.

take: py-tree-sitter gives Python access to incremental tree-sitter parsing, with an examples directory. It is the parser behind enclosing-definition lookups and syntax-aware chunking for the assistant's code retrieval.
why: Chunking code at function boundaries is the cheapest way to cut retrieval noise.
caveat: Needs the grammar packages for each language and a prebuilt wheel for Python 3.12 or later on every platform; the examples directory was listed, not read.
falsifier: Chunk the repository by function and by fixed window and compare recall at 10 on the retrieval set; if function chunks do not beat windows by 3 points, drop it.

take: Zoekt is a trigram-based code search engine in Go with index, query and search packages; it is a reference for substring and regular-expression search over a large repository without embeddings. Its README adds that it ranks results with code-related signals such as whether a match is on a symbol and that it supports boolean query operators.
why: Exact identifier search is the common failure of dense retrieval over code.
caveat: Go program with a large index; for laptop-sized repositories ripgrep may already be enough.
falsifier: Compare identifier queries against ripgrep on the corpus; if latency is not at least 5 times lower at the same recall, drop it.

take: Headroom compresses tool outputs, logs, files and RAG chunks before they reach a model and claims 20 percent fewer tokens for coding agents; it ships as a library, proxy and MCP server. Read for which output kinds it compresses and how it restores them. Its README reports 21 to 57 percent fewer input tokens on four agent scenarios, over 90 percent on repeated JSON arrays and log lines and little on prose, with compression running on the local machine.
why: Tool output fills a small context window; trimming is the cheapest context management.
caveat: Large multi-language repository whose listed paths are build files only; the claimed savings are the project's own; dependency on its Rust core.
falsifier: Apply a similar trimming of test and build logs to 50 sessions; if answer correctness drops by even 1 answer, trimming loses needed text.

take: LLMLingua compresses prompts with a small language model that scores token information; its README claims up to 20x compression with minimal loss. It is a method to test for compressing retrieved context before the local model sees it. Its README news items also list KV-cache work (SCBench, RetrievalAttention, MInference) from the same group.
why: dawnr ask runs on a laptop with limited memory; a compressor needs its own model, which has to pay for itself.
caveat: Requires loading another model; the compression claims come from the authors' benchmarks, not code tasks.
falsifier: Compress retrieved context at 2x with it and measure answer correctness; if it falls by more than 2 points of the question set, drop it.

take: OpenSandbox describes itself as a secure, extensible sandbox runtime for AI agents, with server, SDKs and API specs directories. Its API spec is a reference for what operations a sandbox for model-written code should expose. Its README says sandboxes start locally with Docker or on Kubernetes through one sandbox API and quotes Firecracker creation times of 64 ms median, which are the project's figures.
why: Sandbox operation names and limits (files, commands, timeouts) are a design question for the repository assistant.
caveat: Server-side runtime aimed at Kubernetes and cloud, far heavier than a laptop needs; only the specs matter.
falsifier: Map the spec operations onto the harness runtime; if more than 3 are missing there and needed, note them as work.

take: Lift the pair-mining rule of Break-It-Fix-It: a fixer's output is kept as a new (bad, good) training pair only when an external critic reports zero errors on it and the edit distance from the broken input is between 1 and 4, and a trained breaker makes new bad inputs from good ones. dawnr has a critic stronger than a compiler, the seven-way gate, and a source of broken twins.
why: One round of witness-fed repair moved the gate from 66 to 69 of 182 cells and self-repair from verdicts gave 2 clean of 110; the missing ingredient named in the literature is a candidate repair, and this mines verified candidates.
caveat: Python scripts around parallel text files (train.good, train.bad, train.id) with os.system calls and a docker directory; the critic is a parser or compiler call in the original and would be replaced by the seven-way gate, which is far more expensive per sample.
code_note: generate_paired_data_from_fixer_preds_for_BIFI walks the evaluated prediction files of three splits, keeps a prediction when pred_err_obj == 0 and 0 < diff_metric <= 4, writes parallel id, good and bad files, and asserts the three lists have equal length before writing; predictions that still fail the critic are simply not written.
falsifier: Mine pairs from the 110 repaired answers and the existing 525 repair rows with the gate as critic; if fewer than 20 new pairs survive, or training on them does not move the 66 of 182 cell count by at least 3, it does not help.

take: Lift the mutation catalogue: an ast.NodeTransformer family with named categories (binary operations, comparison, boolean operators, augmented assignment, constants) that proposes the compatible operator replacements at each location. Applied to a problem's reference solution, it gives mutants that a specification must reject.
why: Gate precision is 0.682 against 0.70; the gate requires rejection of at least 60 percent of mutated outputs, but outputs are not programs, and program mutants test the specification against wrong implementations.
caveat: Last push 2023, so its use of the ast module must be checked against Python 3.12; it mutates Python source, while the reference solutions are Python and the t specification needs a separate mapping of the mutated behaviour; the project also has a runner and CLI (run.py, cli.py) that are not meant.
code_note: transformers.py holds a CATEGORIES dictionary, LocIndex and MutationOpSet named tuples, and MutateBase(ast.NodeTransformer) with per-category subclasses; for a comparison node with several operators it mutates only the first and logs the case, so multi-operator comparisons are under-mutated.
falsifier: Generate mutants of the 232 reference solutions, keep those that fail the problem's tests, and run the specification gate on them; if fewer than 10 percent of surviving specifications accept a failing mutant, the stage adds nothing beyond the present mutated-output check.

take: mini-verl runs verl-style PPO, GRPO and on-policy distillation on one NVIDIA GPU with resumable runs and adapter export, and ships environment files for an RTX 4080 on Linux and under WSL2. It is the closest published recipe for training against a verifier's reward on the local card.
why: Verifier-in-the-loop training is named in the research notes, and one RTX 4080 is the local card.
caveat: The README examples use a Qwen3-0.6B model and a toy length reward; a reward from the seven-way gate would need an asynchronous grader since each cell takes seconds to minutes; the README shows an 8-GPU example for the full verl and a separate single-GPU guide.
falsifier: Run its GRPO example with a reward of 'tests pass' on the 200 held-out problems' sibling training set; if the first-sample pass rate does not rise above the starting rate after 200 steps, or memory exceeds 16 GB, it does not help.

take: Repilot filters a language model's next-token choices at each step by asking a completion engine (a modified Eclipse JDT language server over LSP) which continuations are valid, and its CLI has a pruned-mem repair method. It is a worked example of pruning candidate tokens with a type-aware semantic service rather than a grammar.
why: The type and scope restriction planned for the teacher is the same idea; here a language server is the source of in-scope names.
caveat: Java only and needs three JDK versions and a modified JDT server per its README; dawnr would need a t completion service (names and types in scope), which does not exist.
falsifier: Build a stub completion service that returns in-scope names for 20 t problems and prune with it; if valid-completion recall drops below 95 percent of the names that appear in correct answers, pruning excludes right answers.

take: DrRepair repairs programs from compiler diagnostics with a graph over the source tokens and the error message, trained on self-generated corruptions; the model and evaluation directories hold the code. It is a baseline for whether better error messages move repair.
why: The literature names a candidate repair, not a better error message, as the missing ingredient; this is the strongest published error-message-to-fix model to test that against.
caveat: 2020 research code on an older PyTorch; read at README and directory level only.
falsifier: Feed it the Frama-C and Dafny messages of 50 failing cells; if fewer than 3 of 50 are repaired, error-message-driven repair is not the lever.

take: icontract-hypothesis derives Hypothesis test strategies from icontract preconditions, so a function with contracts can be tested automatically with inputs that satisfy them. It could turn the Python reference solution's stated preconditions into an input generator for specification checks.
why: Specification checks need inputs that satisfy a precondition, or they test vacuous cases.
caveat: Last push 2022 and 3.7 era; strategies are filtered from preconditions so tight preconditions produce slow rejection sampling; the contracts must first be written in icontract form.
falsifier: Generate inputs for 30 reference solutions with preconditions; if fewer than 20 of 30 produce 100 valid inputs within 10 seconds, it cannot drive the check.
code_note: make_assume_preconditions builds a function that evaluates a callable's icontract preconditions on given arguments and raises hypothesis.errors.UnsatisfiedAssumption when a precondition group fails; when the function has no preconditions it returns an always-satisfied no-op, so contract-free functions are not rejected.

take: Scarlet learns a linear temporal logic formula that accepts a set of positive traces and rejects negative ones, using a combinatorial search. The twin input pairs (original passes, broken twin fails) are such examples, so it is a way to infer a property from them for comparison with the model's specification.
why: Specification precision depends on whether a specification separates the right outputs from near misses; learning one from the pairs gives an independent reference.
caveat: LTL is for traces, while t specifications relate inputs to outputs, so an encoding is needed; research code with an installation script.
falsifier: Encode 10 twins as traces; if the learned formulas do not separate the twin on all 10, drop it.

take: Angelix repairs C programs from failing tests by symbolic execution (KLEE) and an SMT solver, searching for a minimal change. It is the one tool here that produces a candidate repair for C from constraints rather than from a model. Its README says it searches for the minimal change that preserves the original source and is distributed as source code plus a VirtualBox image.
why: A candidate repair, not a message, is what the literature says is missing; a constraint-derived candidate costs no model call.
caveat: Archived; ships a Dockerfile and submodules around KLEE, so it is unlikely to run on current toolchains without work.
falsifier: Try it on 5 of the fixed PX4 defects with their failing inputs; if it finds the upstream fix in fewer than 2 of 5, drop it.

take: wobbly applies metamorphic checks to extracted numbers so wrong model outputs can be found without an answer key, with no dependencies (Python 3.9 or later). The idea can be applied to extraction outputs in the documents path.
why: Grounded extraction is checked by quotation, and numbers are the part with no quote to compare.
caveat: Six stars; its example is receipts; the writeup is on a blog.
falsifier: Apply its checks to the extraction evaluation set; if it flags fewer wrong numbers than the present quotation check, drop it.

take: Study how hax lowers one source language to Lean, F* and Rocq backends through a pipeline of named rewrite phases, each declaring in types which language features it turns off (for example For_loop, While_loop, Fold_like_loop), with failures raised as diagnostics carrying a source span. It is the nearest published design to dawnr's lowering of t into several proof systems with abstention by name.
why: Lowerings must abstain by name when they cannot express something, and a lowering that silently weakens a specification has already caused errors here.
caveat: OCaml engine plus Rust frontend built with nix or opam and a pinned Rust toolchain; the source language is Rust, so only the architecture of phases and feature flags carries over.
code_note: phase_functionalize_loops.ml includes Features.Off modules for each loop form the phase removes, so later phases cannot receive them by construction; diagnostics.ml defines a fatal Error exception and a raise function that takes the definition id, a context and a span, so a refusal names the construct and where it was.
falsifier: List the constructs each of the 7 lowerings currently refuses and which of those refusals are enforced by a check rather than by convention; if fewer than 2 of the 7 have an unchecked silent path, the pattern fixes nothing measured.

take: Take the strict acceptance rule for Lean output: compile the candidate with a probe that appends #print axioms for each declaration, reject any 'declaration uses sorry' warning, and reject any axiom outside the standard set (propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice), then compare that verdict with the plain exit-code check to flag a hack. dawnr's Lean lowering once left goals for sorryAx to discharge.
why: Proof results must not rest on a tactic chain that succeeds without closing its goal; an axiom audit is a cheap independent test of the Lean kernel's verdict.
caveat: Python wrapper around a lean binary with a timeout; imports a sibling harness module for compilation; the repository describes itself as a recursive-self-improvement project and its README claims were not checked here, only the verification function was read.
code_note: check_lemma writes the code plus '#print axioms <name>' lines, compiles with a timeout, returns False with a stated reason for sorry or for axioms outside STANDARD_AXIOMS, and a Verdict records both the strict status and whether a plain exit code would have accepted, so disagreement is the hack signal.
falsifier: Run the check over the Lean outputs of the 213 verified programs and their 213 broken twins; if any program accepted by the current lowering fails the axiom check, or any twin passes it, the current Lean verdict was wrong and this check helps; if none differs, it adds nothing.

take: Eurydice compiles a subset of Rust to C so that programs verified in Rust can still ship as C. Its output is real C for Rust programs with proofs, giving a stream of C functions that already have specifications on the Rust side for CBMC cases.
why: Native cases need functions with a known intended behaviour; Rust-verified code compiled to C comes with one.
caveat: OCaml project with dune and nix files; it compiles only a subset of Rust.
falsifier: Compile 5 verified Rust functions to C and run the native gate; if the gate reports a counterexample on any original verified function, either the compiler or the proof is wrong and the pair is informative; if 0 of 5 reach a complete verdict, it is not a usable source.

take: Smt.ml is an OCaml frontend that talks to several SMT solvers through one interface, with a bench directory comparing them. The design of one expression language lowered to many solver back ends matches dawnr's need to send the same obligation to Z3 and cvc5 and compare.
why: Several front ends share solvers, so agreement is not independence; sending one formula to different solvers measures that directly.
caveat: OCaml with a Dockerfile and nix files; only the interface idea transfers to Python.
falsifier: Send the obligations of 20 twins to Z3 and cvc5 through a thin Python wrapper; if the two solvers never disagree on any of the 20 obligations, solver diversity gives no new information on this set.

take: Flux is a refinement type checker for Rust whose tests directory holds annotated Rust programs with expected accept and reject results. The accept-and-reject test pairs are a design for a regression suite of verified programs and their broken twins.
why: Each dawnr program has a broken twin that must be refuted; Flux's test layout shows how another verifier organises that pairing.
caveat: Needs a pinned Rust nightly; contents of tests only listed.
falsifier: Count how many of its tests are reject cases; if the reject share is below one third, it is not a model for the twin discipline.

take: Jasmin is a language and compiler for high-assurance cryptography, with a compiler directory and a proofs directory holding the Coq proofs of its passes. It is a reference for pairing a compiler pass with a machine-checked correctness proof.
why: Lowerings have no proof of correctness; seeing a compiler whose passes do is a design reference.
caveat: OCaml and Rocq; no direct code to reuse.
falsifier: Identify one dawnr lowering step small enough to state its preservation theorem; if none can be stated in under 30 lines of Rocq, the approach is too heavy.

take: AXLE is a Python client and CLI for a hosted Lean verification API with environments such as CSLib, with options to extract declarations and simplify. Its client shows which operations a Lean checking service exposes: check, extract and simplify.
why: Lean runs are slow to start; the operation list is a design reference for a persistent Lean checker.
caveat: Depends on a hosted service run by the company, so it cannot be a local dependency; the client code only is relevant.
falsifier: Compare its check operation's latency with a local lake build for the 213 programs; if the hosted call is not faster, drop it.

take: Rocq proofs about OSS-Fuzz fuzz targets compiled to binaries, stating that no input within stated limits makes the sanitizer build misbehave. They show how a safety property of a compiled C program is stated as a theorem rather than as a bounded check.
why: Bounded checks give no statement beyond the bound; this is a published unbounded alternative statement form.
caveat: The README says each proof is about compiled binaries on every input within stated limits, not about source; the proofs and theories directories were listed, not read; the build needs the project's Rocq model of a Linux process.
falsifier: State the same property for one wrap_bin binary in the same form; if the statement needs more than the SMT bit-vector facts CBMC already proves, it is out of reach.

take: Use Estimator::integrate_angular_rate as a second autopilot function for the flight correspondence work: it propagates a quaternion in single-precision float by a matrix-exponential step or an Euler step, with its own turbomath library for trigonometry. In the matrix-exponential branch the four quaternion assignments read components already overwritten earlier in the same block; whether that matters numerically has not been tested.
why: Flight checks use binary64 where production uses binary32; this firmware is float throughout and ships its own unit tests to compare against.
caveat: C++ class bound to a ROSflight object for parameters, so the function must be extracted with the parameter read replaced by a constant for each branch; BSD-3-Clause for the repository, but the vendored libraries under lib/ may have their own terms and were not checked; the file is a source for a case, not a verified specification.
code_note: integrate_angular_rate returns at once when the squared rate norm is exactly 0.0f; otherwise the matrix-exponential branch computes sqrtf, cosf and sinf of half the rotation angle in float and normalises the result, and the other branch forms a quaternion derivative and adds it scaled by dt; no assertion or error path exists for a non-finite rate.
falsifier: Write the native case for both branches in binary32 and compare with a binary64 version on 1,000 sampled inputs; if the largest difference in the normalised quaternion is under 1e-6 for both branches, binary32 versus binary64 does not matter here and the case adds no information on that gap.

take: Daisy is a Scala tool whose analysis directory has range, absolute-error, relative-error and FPTaylor phases for rounding error of floating-point programs, with a testcases directory. It gives a rigorous round-off bound to compare against the sampled binary32 versus binary64 differences of the flight checks.
why: Flight checks use binary64 where production uses binary32 and the size of the gap is not bounded.
caveat: Needs Java 22 to 25, a C compiler and MPFR per its README; input is Daisy's own Scala-like language, so each function must be re-expressed.
falsifier: Bound the round-off of 3 flight functions with it; if the proven bound is more than 100 times the largest sampled error, the bound is too loose to decide anything.

take: Kind 2 is an SMT-based model checker for safety properties of Lustre programs, the dataflow language of control software; its README recommends Z3 for integer and real variables. It would check discrete control logic such as hysteresis and mode switching that the flight twins model. Its README adds that results come as JSON or XML and that it runs bounded model checking and induction processes in parallel, returning an input sequence for each falsified property.
why: Hysteresis and switch logic in the flight files are state machines over time, which bounded single-call checks cover only for one step.
caveat: OCaml; requires re-expressing the t program in Lustre; not an obvious fit for numerical functions.
falsifier: Encode the hysteresis_update program and prove one invariant; if the encoding takes more than a day, the cost exceeds the benefit.

take: pyulog parses ULog files, the self-describing flight log format of PX4, with scripts such as ulog_info. Real logged inputs of an estimator or controller would give realistic input ranges for the sampled comparisons instead of uniform ranges.
why: Bounded input comparisons miss the region where the vehicle actually flies; logged values define that region.
caveat: Needs actual log files, which this repository does not ship in its code path; BSD-3-Clause for the parser.
falsifier: Replay 10,000 logged states through the compiled and fixed code; if no divergence appears that sampled inputs did not already find, logs add nothing.

take: F Prime is NASA's component framework for flight software in C++, with service components under Svc and framework base types under Fw. Its component layout is a reference for which kinds of flight code have simple pure functions that can be lifted into cases.
why: Flight-domain coverage currently rests on PX4 files alone; a second code base reduces that dependence.
caveat: Large; the listed directories were not opened beyond their names.
falsifier: Pick 3 pure functions under Svc and build cases; if fewer than 2 have inputs of at most 64 bits, drop it.

take: MiniCheck scores whether each claim is supported by a document, chunking long documents, with small encoder checkpoints (roberta-large, deberta-v3-large, flan-t5-large) selectable by name beside its 7B model. It is a groundedness judge that could check citations in locallm/cite_docs.py without a large model.
why: Citation output is checked only by quotation presence; a claim can quote a real sentence and still not be supported by it.
caveat: The repository has a synthetic_data_gen directory and the provenance of the checkpoints' training data was not checked, so it may serve as a judge but its data must not be used for training dawnr until that is checked; the 7B option needs vLLM, the small ones need transformers and a GPU or slow CPU runs.
