code_note: MiniCheck.__init__ asserts the model name is one of five allowed values and loads either a vLLM model or an encoder; score(docs, claims, chunk_size) returns a probability per pair after splitting long documents into chunks; an unknown model name fails fast with an AssertionError listing the options.
falsifier: Score 200 answer-claim pairs from the citation evaluation with deberta-v3-large; if agreement with human labels is under 85 percent, or the check takes more than 1 second per claim on the laptop, it does not help.

take: docling-parse extracts characters, words and lines from programmatic PDFs together with their page coordinates, in C++ with a Python package. Coordinates give a citation a position in the page as well as a quoted string.
why: Grounded extraction needs a span the reader can find; a bounding box is stronger than a substring match.
caveat: C++ build with CMake and a prebuilt wheel question for Python 3.12 or later on Windows; only works for text-based PDFs, not scans.
falsifier: Locate 100 quoted extraction spans in 20 PDFs by coordinate; if fewer than 95 are found at the right place, drop it.

take: PDFOxide is a Rust PDF library with a Python package, text extraction and a claim of 0.8 ms mean per document. If that holds on the extraction corpus it replaces a slower reader in the document path. Its README describes a Rust core with bindings for 19 languages and a CLI.
why: Document reading time counts toward the cold start of dawnr ask.
caveat: Speed figures are the project's; a wheel for each platform must be checked; many language bindings add repository size.
falsifier: Time it against the present reader on the 50 test PDFs; if it is not at least 3 times faster or text differs on more than 2, drop it.

take: A fork of OSS-Fuzz that adds hybrid fuzzing with dynamic symbolic execution, with a projects directory of open-source targets and a TROPHIES.md list of defects found. The trophies list is a record of real bugs with the target that exposed them. Its README says each project provides fuzz targets for libFuzzer, AFL++ and Sydr, a build script, a dictionary, an initial seed corpus, a Dockerfile and a hybrid-fuzzing configuration file, which is a ready set of entry points and corpora per project.
why: The gate has found few real defects; a list of confirmed defects with their projects shows which kinds of C bugs a symbolic engine finds.
caveat: Docker-heavy; the defects found are in whole programs reached from fuzz entry points, not scalar functions.
falsifier: Take 10 trophy bugs in functions with scalar inputs and write cases; if the gate finds fewer than 5, it is missing bug classes.

take: The Arbitrary trait builds a typed value from an unstructured byte slice, with a derive macro for structs and enums. The byte-slice-to-typed-value design is the model for turning one nondeterministic buffer into the scalar inputs of a harness and back for replay. Its README says it turns the raw byte buffers a fuzzer produces into well-typed structured values, to combine structure-aware generation with coverage-guided mutation.
why: Replaying a counterexample natively needs inputs as bit patterns; an Arbitrary-style decoder defines one byte layout for both CBMC and the replay binary.
caveat: Rust crate; only the decoding design transfers to a C harness.
falsifier: Define the byte layout for 5 cases and replay; if any native replay input differs from the CBMC trace value, the layout is wrong.

take: Gophersat is a SAT and pseudo-Boolean solver in Go with an explain directory for minimal unsatisfiable subsets (mus.md in the tree). A minimal unsatisfiable core of the assumptions explains why a case is complete or vacuous. Its README says it runs about 2 to 5 times slower than top solvers on typical SAT benchmarks, also solves MAXSAT and pseudo-Boolean problems and has an optional cutting-planes strategy.
why: Vacuity is currently found by counting unreachable coverage goals; a core would name the assumptions responsible.
caveat: Go binary or library; CBMC's formula would have to be exported; cores are for CNF, not for CBMC assumptions directly.
falsifier: Extract a core for the vacuous control (assume(0 != 0)); if the core does not contain that assumption, it does not explain vacuity.

take: Ready-made CMake modules that add AddressSanitizer, UBSan, thread and leak sanitizer build types, AFL fuzzing targets and code coverage to a C or C++ project. They would provide the sanitizer flags for the native replay build of real projects.
why: Native replay compiles with sanitizers by hand-written commands per case; real projects need their build system to carry them.
caveat: CMake only; the project must use CMake; Apache-2.0 notice must be kept.
falsifier: Build 3 CMake projects with sanitizers using these modules; if fewer than 3 build without edits, drop it.

take: SAW verifies C and other code against specifications using symbolic simulation; its tree includes a cve-reports directory and s2nTests alongside examples. The CVE reports are write-ups of real defects found or checked with the tool, with the specification that exposes each. Its README points to two tutorials, one for verifying C (through LLVM) and Java code and one for Rust.
why: Finding-to-case cost is the bottleneck; specifications of known CVEs show how others state the property.
caveat: Haskell, built with cabal and several solver dependencies; the directories were listed, not read.
falsifier: Re-state 3 CVE specifications as CBMC cases; if CBMC cannot reproduce the defect in 2 of 3, the specification style does not transfer.

take: PASTIS runs several fuzzers and symbolic engines on one target and exchanges seeds through a broker (pastisbroker, libpastis). The seed-exchange protocol is a design for passing CBMC witnesses to fuzzers and back. Its README lists Honggfuzz, AFL++ and TritonDSE as supported engines and an installation by pip (pastis-framework).
why: A counterexample from CBMC could seed native fuzzing to find sibling inputs, and fuzz crashes could be handed to CBMC for a case.
caveat: Python with Docker and several engine dependencies; not designed for a bounded model checker. TritonDSE is the symbolic engine, not a bounded model checker.
falsifier: Seed a fuzzer with CBMC witnesses for 3 cases; if it finds no input beyond the seeds in 10 minutes, the exchange adds nothing.

take: gllvm builds whole-program LLVM bitcode for a C project by wrapping the compiler, in parallel, as a drop-in for wllvm. It supplies bitcode of real projects for LLVM-based verifiers such as Symbiotic or SeaHorn-style tools.
why: Whole-program bitcode is the input form of several verifiers dawnr could add as second opinions.
caveat: Last push 2024-04; Go program; Linux and macOS; Windows not an intended platform.
falsifier: Build bitcode for one pinned PX4 source subset; if the build requires more than manual wrapper settings, drop it.

take: Theta is a Java modular model-checking framework from Budapest with several abstraction-refinement algorithms and integration tests. It is one more independent engine for C programs through its subprojects, for a third opinion beside CBMC and CPAchecker. Its README describes abstraction-refinement algorithms with pluggable front ends, abstract domains and strategies, usable as a back end or as stand-alone tools.
why: Single-engine verdicts carry the engine's blind spots.
caveat: Gradle build on the JVM; C support goes through a front end in a subproject that was not inspected.
falsifier: Run on 5 controls; if it matches CBMC on fewer than 4, it is not a usable cross-check.

take: Glucose 4.2.1 is a CDCL SAT solver based on MiniSat 2.2, with core, simp and parallel directories. As a third, older-lineage solver it widens the cross-solver check on native formulas beyond CaDiCaL and Kissat.
why: Solver diversity is the available substitute for a proof certificate.
caveat: C++ built with CMake or make; no LRAT output claimed in the files read.
falsifier: Solve all native formulas with it and CaDiCaL; if the two never disagree on any of them, a third solver adds nothing.

take: A directory of fuzzing dictionaries for file formats such as gif, html, http and csv, usable to seed inputs for string and parser functions. Dictionary tokens give the keywords for replay inputs of text-parsing cases. Its documentation list includes a note on how to split a fuzzer-generated input into parts, which is the question of mapping one byte buffer to several scalar inputs.
why: Native replay of a parser witness benefits from realistic tokens instead of random bytes.
caveat: Format-specific; Apache-2.0; scalar-input cases rarely need it. The repository is archived.
falsifier: Use dictionary tokens for 5 parser cases; if replay finds no more crashes than random inputs in 1,000 tries, drop it.

take: Symbiotic instruments a program for a property, slices it with a static slicer and runs KLEE; the properties directory holds the SV-COMP property files and the sbt-slicer submodule listed at the root is the slicer. Slicing a large function down to the statements that influence an assertion is a way to shrink a harness before CBMC.
why: Loops bounded by hand cost the most when the function is large; slicing removes code that cannot affect the property.
caveat: LLVM-based, built from submodules (klee, dg, llvm2c) with a Dockerfile; Linux oriented; slicing changes the code CBMC sees, so a sliced verdict is not a verdict on the original.
falsifier: Slice 5 cases at their assertion and compare verdicts with the unsliced run; if any verdict differs, slicing is unsafe for the gate.

take: Use the AdamW schedule-free optimizer, which replaces the learning-rate schedule with an iterate average and takes only a warmup_steps argument. Because it needs no decay horizon, a locallm run can be stopped, evaluated and continued without choosing the total step count first.
why: Training budget is limited and runs are continued from checkpoints; a schedule tied to a fixed length is a source of waste in each continuation.
caveat: The optimizer must be switched with .train() before training steps and .eval() before evaluation or saving a checkpoint to be used for inference, otherwise the evaluated weights are the wrong iterate; optimizer state must be saved and restored with the checkpoint.
code_note: The class docstring states that .train() and .eval() must be called before training and evaluation; eval() reads the per-group train_mode flag, and the constructor takes warmup_steps and weight_lr_power instead of a schedule object.
falsifier: Train the locallm size twice on the same token budget, once with the current AdamW plus schedule and once with this optimizer; if held-out validation loss differs by less than 0.02 nats in its favour, or the checkpoint saved after eval() scores worse than the one saved before, it does not help.

take: Lift speculative_decode: a small draft model proposes speculate_k tokens one at a time, the target model scores the proposal plus the current token in one forward pass, and each draft token is accepted with probability min(1, q/p). A trained locallm model could draft for a larger model, or the reverse, to cut the latency of dawnr ask.
why: dawnr ask takes 64.6 s from a cold start; decode latency is a part that speculative decoding addresses and the acceptance rule preserves the target distribution.
caveat: PyTorch code that takes input positions and block masks and does not run through llama.cpp, which is how the GGUF model is served, so only the algorithm transfers; needs a draft and a target model with the same tokenizer.
code_note: speculative_decode computes draft probabilities p and target probabilities q on the proposed tokens, accepts all when no sampled uniform exceeds min(1, q/p), then samples one more token from the last target distribution and feeds it to the draft model; the remainder of the function was not read.
falsifier: Measure tokens per second with a locallm draft and the 27B-class teacher or a mid-size target on the laptop; if the acceptance rate is under 50 percent or the speedup is under 1.3 times, it does not help.

take: T-MAC runs low-bit LLM inference on CPUs with lookup tables instead of dequantisation and its README compares tokens per second against llama.cpp on a laptop and an M2 Ultra. It is a measured alternative for the CPU-only laptop path of dawnr ask.
why: Cold-start time and peak memory on a laptop without a strong GPU decide whether dawnr ask is usable.
caveat: Requires converting models to its own low-bit format and building native kernels; the README results are for BitNet and Phi-3.5, not for a model trained here.
falsifier: Run locallm's quantised model with it and with llama.cpp on the same laptop CPU; if tokens per second is less than 1.2 times llama.cpp's, it does not help.

take: MiniCPM publishes small on-device models with a finetune directory, a quantize directory and tool_parsers for function calls. The finetune and quantize scripts are a worked small-model path from training to quantised on-device use.
why: The local model is small and must be quantised for the laptop; this is a documented path for a comparable size.
caveat: Targets Hugging Face transformers checkpoints; README is bilingual; the directories were listed but not read.
falsifier: Apply its quantize recipe to the locallm checkpoint; if held-out clean answers fall by more than 1 of 232, the recipe loses accuracy at this size.

take: minbpe trains a byte-level BPE vocabulary with an optional regular-expression pre-split pattern and has a tests directory with a sample text file. Its tests are the pattern to extend into an encode-decode integrity check that guards against silent loss of spaces.
why: A tokenizer has silently eaten text before in this project; a compact reference with round-trip tests is the cheapest guard.
caveat: Pure Python and slow on large corpora; the repository is an educational implementation, with a train.py script.
falsifier: Run encode-decode tests on all training and held-out t files with each tokenizer in use; if any file fails to round-trip, the check has found a defect.

take: bpeasy trains a BPE vocabulary in about 400 lines of Rust behind a Python package, following the Hugging Face tokenizers design. It would train a vocabulary specialised to t source and C in minutes for tokenizer experiments.
why: Whether a code-specific vocabulary reduces tokens per program is a cheap experiment before a training round.
caveat: Needs a Rust-built wheel for each platform; output vocabulary must be converted for use with llama.cpp.
falsifier: Train a 8k vocabulary on the t corpus and compare tokens per program with the current tokenizer; if the reduction is under 10 percent, it does not help.

take: TokenMonster trains an ungreedy subword vocabulary and publishes a benchmark pretraining 16 language models on different tokenizers. The benchmark directory is a source of evidence about whether tokenizer choice moves model quality at small scale. Its README links vocabularies named englishcode with sizes of 16,000 and 24,000 tokens, so code-oriented vocabularies are among those compared.
why: Small models are sensitive to tokenizer choice; evidence from controlled pretraining runs is rare.
caveat: The benchmark is the author's, on English text; it does not test code.
falsifier: Re-run the comparison for two vocabularies on a locallm-size model; if validation loss differs by under 1 percent, tokenizer choice is not the lever.

take: LitData streams optimised datasets for training and its README lists parallel data processing and streaming without preparation. It is one option for resumable streaming of token shards from disk on one machine. Its README lists pausing and resuming data streaming and streaming remote data without local loading.
why: Training on one RTX 4080 is limited by data loading when shards are large; streaming with resume state avoids repeats.
caveat: Own binary shard format; heavy dependency tree; locallm already has shard code, so the gain is untested.
falsifier: Compare step time with the existing loader on the same shards; if it is not at least 10 percent faster, drop it.

take: BMTrain is an efficient training library for pre-training and fine-tuning with ZeRO-style parameter sharding. Its bmtrain package is a reference for sharding and checkpointing when a model plus optimizer state does not fit one card.
why: One RTX 4080 has 16 GB; optimizer state sharding or offload decides the largest model it can train.
caveat: Aimed at multi-GPU clusters; offers little on a single card beyond offload ideas.
falsifier: Estimate the optimizer-state memory saved on one card; if it is less than 20 percent, drop it.

take: Lift two curation steps: clean_data.py drops a row whose whitespace-stripped instruction or response was already seen and, with an option, whose concatenated function names were already seen (skipping rows whose code block has a syntax error), and find_substrings.py removes rows containing benchmark strings, matched case-insensitively. They would give the teacher rows a duplicate filter by function signature and a substring decontamination pass.
why: Teacher recipes added zero rows in the pilots; a dedup rule keyed by function names shows how many accepted rows are the same problem repeated, and the 32 contaminated problems show decontamination matters.
caveat: Rows are instruction-response pairs of Python and the function-name key is Python specific (an ast visitor), so for t the key would be the signature; the pipeline around these files used a language model for generation, whose outputs must follow dawnr's rule on model-written data; the decontamination reads benchmark strings it downloads.
code_note: clean_data.py reads jsonl files, keeps only keys common to all rows, shuffles with a fixed seed, and walks the rows keeping a set of seen keys; a row whose first code block fails to parse is skipped instead of raising, and instruction, response and function-name keys are all added to the same set.
falsifier: Apply the signature-key dedup to the 6,954-row training input; if it removes fewer than 1 percent of rows, or the rows removed include any with a distinct specification, it does not help.

take: Lift the two-stage detection of rephrased contamination: a sentence-transformer retrieves the top-k nearest training case for each test case (vector_db.py), then a language-model judge decides whether the pair is a rephrase of the same problem (llm_detect.py). It extends the n-gram check that found 32 same-task problems to paraphrases.
why: The 200 held-out problems without a same-task source were found by a source-matching procedure; paraphrased copies in the 6,954 training rows would inflate learning claims.
caveat: The default judge is an OpenAI model named gpt-4 and the script checks for an OpenAI key, so the judge must be swapped for a non-excluded model and labels from GPT models must not be training data; last push 2023-12; MiniLM embeddings from sentence-transformers.
code_note: main.py parses train, test and output paths, a bert model name (default multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1), top_k (default 1), a data type (default code) and worker count, builds a database of top-k similar cases and then calls llm_detect with a thread pool; check_openai_key aborts early if no key is set.
falsifier: Run it with a local judge on the 232 held-out problems against the training rows; if it flags fewer than the 32 already known contaminated problems, or flags more than 10 not in that list that a person confirms are unrelated, it does not help.

take: SemHash performs semantic deduplication, outlier filtering and representative-sample selection over text records, with a small API (semhash.py, index.py). It could remove near-duplicate natural-language problems among the teacher rows and choose a representative subset when only a few can be trained on.
why: The matched-examples retrieval planned for the teacher needs a measure of how close two problems are; the same measure finds redundant rows.
caveat: Embedding model dependence; works on text so code similarity is not covered; Python 3.12 wheel support was not checked.
falsifier: Run it on the teacher problem descriptions at a 0.9 similarity threshold; if the duplicate groups it finds are not at least 20 percent larger than those from exact normalised-text matching, it adds nothing.
code_note: from_records first groups records by key and embeds only the deduplicated ones, and from_embeddings raises ValueError for empty records, a non-2D embedding array, a count mismatch, or missing columns for dictionary records; vectors go into an approximate-nearest-neighbour index chosen by a backend argument.

take: R2E-Gym generates software-engineering environments procedurally and combines execution-based and execution-free verifiers to rank candidate patches at test time, with train and reproduction directories. The hybrid verifier idea is a published way to pick among sampled repairs. Its README links data and models on the Hugging Face Hub and reproduction guides in a reproduction folder.
why: Answer rate may be a search budget before it is a training problem; selecting among many repair samples needs a verifier-based ranking.
caveat: Targets Python repositories and Docker environments; code was not read.
falsifier: Rank 10 repairs per failing cell with the seven-way gate versus a model score; if gate-only ranking is not at least as good, drop the hybrid.

take: Repo2RLEnv turns a repository into verifiable reinforcement-learning tasks for coding agents that can be trained on, evaluated and shared on the Hugging Face Hub. It is a reference for packaging a task, its test and its verifier together as one unit. Its README states the need as thousands of tasks, each with a working environment, an instruction that does not give the answer away and a verifier you can trust, and names Tasksmith, pipelines and datasets as parts.
why: A dawnr training row is a problem, an answer and a pile of gates; a standard task packaging helps reproduction.
caveat: Focused on repository tasks and Harbor; packaging code only.
falsifier: Package 10 dawnr problems in its format; if the verifier cannot express the seven-way gate result, drop it.

take: airoboros implements the Self-Instruct pipeline and ships an example-config.yaml and a scripts directory. Its configuration file is a template for varying the types of problems a teacher is asked to write. Its README says the approach does not use human-generated seeds and supports the completions and chat-completions endpoints including GPT models, whose outputs dawnr must not train on.
why: Coverage of problem kinds in teacher data decides which parts of t get exercised.
caveat: Last push 2024-03; its README describes using models whose outputs may not be trained on; the pipeline code only is meant. Only the pipeline structure is usable.
falsifier: Generate 100 problems from an adapted config; if fewer than 30 are new to the current corpus, coverage does not widen.

take: The curation code of The Stack v2 and the extra StarCoder2 sources, with directories the_stack, spark, ir, kaggle and pull_requests_and_issues. It is a reference for how a public code corpus is assembled from several sources. Its README calls it a follow-up of the bigcode-dataset repository used for The Stack v1.
why: Assembling a corpus from several sources with a recorded script is the discipline dawnr's rows lack outside t.
caveat: Built for terabyte scale on Spark; only the filtering logic is of interest to a 7,000 row corpus.
falsifier: Re-create its source-assembly steps for dawnr's C and t corpora; if the resulting corpus cannot be rebuilt byte for byte from the script, it does not help.

take: Data preparation for the Amber 7B model, with a mix_and_split script, a validate_json script and good and bad sample files showing what passes validation. It is a compact example of a documented mixture recipe whose validator has both accepted and rejected sample files. Its README lists the steps as download, tokenize with the LLaMA tokenizer, concatenate into 2048-token sequences, then merge and split.
why: Locallm's mixture of t data, source code and prose should be reproducible from a script with a validator.
caveat: Uses RedPajama sources and a list of StarCoder languages; scale is far above dawnr's.
falsifier: Write the equivalent mixture script for locallm; if its output differs from the shards used in the last run, the record was incomplete.

take: This is the implementation of the paper Detecting Pretraining Data from Large Language Models, with a src directory, a data processing script and a mink_prob figure. It can test whether a held-out problem was seen by a base model without needing its training set. Its README links the WikiMIA and BookMIA benchmarks and names the method Min-K% Prob.
why: The 232 held-out problems are MBPP, which base models almost certainly saw; a membership signal would put a number on it.
caveat: Needs token log-probabilities from the base model; the paper's results are for English web text; research code from 2023.
falsifier: Score MBPP and a set of freshly written problems with a base model; if the two score distributions overlap by more than 80 percent, it cannot detect exposure.

take: Lift the two paired tests in significance.py: bootstrap resampling of per-item statistics with a seeded generator (default seed 12345, overridable by an environment variable) and a paired approximate randomization test whose p-value is (c+1)/(n+1) with a strict greater-than so a system compared to itself is not called significant. They are metric-independent skeletons for comparing two answer sets on the same problems.
why: Three rounds tied Phi-4-mini at 3 of 232; a paired test with a recorded seed puts a p-value on such ties instead of a count.
caveat: Written around machine-translation metrics (Metric objects and hypothesis/reference lists), so the resampling core must be extracted and fed per-problem 0/1 outcomes; it adds multi-process options not needed; Apache-2.0 notice kept if vendored.
code_note: _bootstrap_resample draws n_samples index arrays with rng.choice(replace=True) from a numpy Generator seeded by SACREBLEU_SEED (12345 by default, entropy if set to none); _compute_p_value counts samples strictly greater than the real difference and applies the +1 correction, citing the multeval test it was taken from.
falsifier: Apply the paired approximate randomization test to the existing 3 of 232 versus 2 of 232 comparison; if it reports p below 0.05 for a difference of one answer, the test is mis-implemented; if it reports p above 0.5 as expected, it correctly shows the tie is not evidence.

take: SWT-Bench scores a generated test by whether it fails on the original code and passes after the fix, a fail-to-pass criterion computed by an evaluation harness in src. The same criterion applied to a specification's tests against a problem's correct and broken programs is the twin discipline in another setting.
why: A test that always passes proves nothing; a fail-to-pass requirement measures whether generated checks discriminate.
caveat: Python repositories and Docker-based execution; the harness is for GitHub issues.
falsifier: Apply fail-to-pass scoring to the model-written tests for 50 training problems; if more than 10 percent already satisfy it trivially via a crash, the tests are weaker than counted.

take: ranx evaluates and compares ranking runs with NumPy and Numba metrics and a compare function for several runs. It would score the local retrieval package's recall and rank metrics across configurations on the same queries.
why: Retrieval changes (BM25 variants, chunking) are only compared by a recall figure; a comparison function over runs makes differences testable.
caveat: Numba dependency must support Python 3.12 or later on all three platforms; last push 2025-08.
falsifier: Re-score the existing retrieval evaluation with it; if its recall at 10 differs from the current script by more than 0.1 point, one of the two is wrong, and if the Fisher and Student tests disagree on significance for a 1-point recall difference, report both.
code_note: compare() in ranx/meta/compare.py takes a stat_test argument ('student' for a two-sided paired Student's t-test by default, 'fisher' for Fisher's randomization test), n_permutations (1000) and max_p (0.01), and marks a system's score significant only when its p-value is under max_p; the choice of test is explicit and documented in the docstring.

take: VeriRun is pre-alpha infrastructure for reproducible isolated execution evaluation; it has a BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md at the root plus schemas and evidence directories. The schemas of evidence records are a reference for what a run should store to be replayable.
why: Every number in dawnr links to a script; a recorded evidence schema extends that to inputs, environment and seeds.
caveat: Marked pre-alpha by its own README; Ray and Docker oriented; only schemas are of interest. Its README warns that the local executor of v0.1 is for trusted fixtures only and is not a security boundary, so model-generated code must not run there.
falsifier: Describe one dawnr run in its schema; if more than 3 required fields cannot be filled from existing logs, the record is incomplete.

take: Can-Ai-Code runs small programming interviews against model outputs and keeps extract.py to pull code from a reply and sbox for sandboxed execution of the result. Its extraction step is a real-world list of the ways model replies wrap code.
why: Parse failures start with extraction; a catalogue of reply shapes shows which formats the tolerant reader has to handle.
caveat: Python tasks; the README is a long essay; code not read.
falsifier: Run its extraction on 1,000 recorded replies; if it recovers fewer parseable answers than the current reader, drop it.

take: TestExplora benchmarks whether language models find bugs proactively by generating repository-level tests, with baseline prompts from its paper. It frames bug discovery as test generation that must expose a defect, like finding a function's break with a case. Its README has sections on setup, test generation inference, supported models and building the benchmark.
why: The task of exposing a defect with a test is the same shape as refuting a twin at a concrete input.
caveat: 16 stars, Python repositories; baseline prompts only.
falsifier: Run the baseline prompt on 20 twin pairs; if the model refutes fewer than half, test generation for twins needs more than prompting.

take: Lift the 57-line loop that keeps a Lark LALR parser beside the model: after each chunk it asks the parser's interactive mode for the terminals that may come next (parse_interactive, exhaust_lexer, accepts), turns each terminal into its regular expression, and has a regex-constrained generator produce only that terminal. It is the smallest working example of grammar-valid decoding one terminal at a time, readable in one sitting before building a prefix check for t.
why: The parse wall means the fix has to sit at generation; a terminal-at-a-time loop is the least invasive version and works with any tokenizer through a regex-guided sampler.
caveat: Depends on the rellm package and transformers, last push 2024-03; one terminal per step is slow and ignores tokens that span terminals; it re-parses the whole partial completion each step; Lark's LALR mode needs t's grammar to be LALR-compatible.
code_note: ParserState.next_lex tries parser.parse on the partial text and, on UnexpectedInput, takes parse_interactive(...).accepts() after exhausting the lexer; complete_cf stops when no terminal is acceptable or only $END is, and otherwise calls complete_re with the allowed terminals' regexes; errors other than UnexpectedInput propagate.
falsifier: Port it to the t grammar and decode the 232 held-out problems; if the share of parse failures stays above 50 percent of unconstrained, or decode time per answer exceeds 10 times the unconstrained time, it does not help.

take: The official tree-sitter grammar for C gives incremental, error-tolerant parsing of C. It would find function boundaries when extracting a function from a source for a native case, and check that a model-drafted harness body parses before it is sent to CBMC.
why: The native case extractor requires each line range to be exactly one function, macro or declaration; a parser makes that check exact instead of brace counting.
caveat: The generated parser needs the tree-sitter runtime and Python bindings for each platform; it parses C without preprocessing, so macros can confuse boundaries.
falsifier: Run it over the pinned PX4 and 4 other sources already used for cases; if it disagrees with the hand-chosen ranges on more than 1 function, brace counting is not the problem.

take: The tree-sitter grammar for C++, an extension of the C grammar. It is the parser needed to extract member functions and templates, the first step toward any native case for a C++ function. Its README shows packages on crates.io, npm and PyPI, so a Python install is available.
why: A C++ function has no case at all; extraction of its definition from a class is the first missing step.
caveat: Parsing only; semantics (overload resolution, templates) are not resolved; same runtime dependencies as the C grammar.
falsifier: Extract 10 member functions from PX4 C++ files; if fewer than 8 are located exactly, extraction by grammar is not enough.

take: A Cython plugin that reimplements Lark's LALR parser and lexer for speed. If a Lark-based prefix check for t is too slow inside a decoding loop, this is the drop-in speedup to measure. Its README says tokens do not inherit from str (use the value attribute) and that postlexers are not implemented, so grammars that use a postlexer cannot take the speedup.
why: Per-token grammar checks run in the generation loop, where parser latency directly adds to answer time.
caveat: Needs a C compiler at install time; last push 2025-07; compatible with Lark LALR only.
falsifier: Time a prefix check on the longest t program with and without it; if the speedup is under 3 times, drop it.

take: A REST server with an OpenAI-compatible API that applies llguidance constraints in front of TensorRT-LLM, written in Rust, with model_configs for each model. Its request handling shows how a constraint (JSON schema, regex or grammar) is attached per request in a server. Its README says the server supports JSON-schema enforcement and full context-free grammars through llguidance and the Guidance library.
why: The local model is served through llama.cpp, and per-request constraints need an API shape; this is a worked example of one.
caveat: TensorRT-LLM needs NVIDIA server GPUs and Linux; only the API design transfers.
falsifier: Express the constraint request shape as a llama.cpp server call; if the server cannot accept a grammar per request, the design does not transfer.

take: Study how a Python generator emits SPARK Ada from a model: it builds Precondition and Postcondition nodes, Ghost declarations and a Loop_Invariant pragma as typed syntax objects, so every generated subprogram carries a contract and a loop invariant that GNATprove must discharge. The construction of Loop_Invariant and Ghost items is the reference for dawnr's SPARK lowering.
why: The SPARK relu_all twin exhausts its budget; a generator that places loop invariants and ghost code by construction is a model for fixing that lowering.
caveat: Large Python plus Rust (rapidflux) tool with a Poetry build; the generated Ada targets message parsing, not arithmetic; code was read only as matches on Precondition, Postcondition and Loop_Invariant in the parser generator.
code_note: parser.py imports Ghost, Precondition and Postcondition from the Ada AST helpers and builds PragmaStatement('Loop_Invariant', [loop_invariant]) inside loop generation; each generated function gets its contracts at construction, so there is no path that emits a body without one.
falsifier: Re-emit the relu_all loop with an invariant in this style and run GNATprove with the same 300 second budget; if the budget is still exhausted, the invariant placement is not the cause.

take: Study the Python-to-Lean target: a LeanTranspiler class that walks the Python AST with visit_ methods, collects class invariants from an if-invariant block, types parameters by an inference pass, and raises AstNotImplementedError with the offending node when a construct has no translation. The same package has a pysmt target, so one Python source is lowered to two proof-adjacent languages by the same machinery.
why: Lowerings must refuse by name what they cannot express; this is a compact open example of a visitor-based lowering with a typed refusal exception, applied to Lean and SMT.
caveat: The Lean output is aimed at Python programs with simple types and may use Lean features that differ from dawnr's pinned toolchain; the repository is large with many language targets; only the Lean and SMT directories matter.
code_note: exceptions.py defines AstErrorBase (message plus ast node), AstNotImplementedError (a NotImplementedError subclass) and AstUnrecognisedBinOp carrying both operand types; the Lean transpiler's visit_FunctionDef builds the signature from inferred types and prefixes method names with the class name, so an unsupported node fails with a node-located exception instead of silently omitting code.
falsifier: Run its Lean and SMT targets over the 232 reference Python solutions; if fewer than 20 translate and compile in Lean, or if any translated function disagrees with its Python original on 20 sampled inputs, it does not help as a cross-check.

take: Storm is a black-box mutational fuzzer for SMT solvers: it takes seed SMT-LIB files and a solver binary and mutates the files to look for crashes and wrong answers. Run against the Z3 and cvc5 versions the seven kernels use, it tests whether a solver bug could be behind a disagreement.
why: Several front ends share solvers, so a shared solver bug would show as agreement; fuzzing the solver directly measures that risk.
caveat: Last push 2020 and its README asks for Python 3.7 and virtualenv, so it needs porting for 3.12; seed files must be collected from the lowerings' SMT output.
falsifier: Fuzz the pinned Z3 for one hour on 20 seeds from the lowerings; if it finds any wrong answer, shared solvers are a live risk; if none after 1,000 mutants, the risk is not evident at this scale.

take: Canonical exhaustively searches for terms of a dependent type, packaged as a Lean tactic with a Rust implementation. Calling it on goals that the Lean lowering leaves open tests whether bounded exhaustive proof search closes more of them than the current tactic chain.
why: Proof automation for Lean is one of the kernels' open failures; a sound and complete inhabitation search is a different strategy from rewriting tactics.
caveat: Needs the Rust crate built or the pre-built package matched to the Lean toolchain version; applicable to goals expressible as types without heavy arithmetic.
falsifier: Run it on the unproved Lean goals of the existing cells; if it closes none of them in 60 seconds each, it adds nothing to the current tactics.

take: Peano is a small proof environment for learning formal mathematical reasoning from scratch, with a foundation, theories, an environment API and a learning directory. Its minimal kernel is a model of a checked step-by-step proof interface for training a small model. Its README describes a dependent type system and a finitely axiomatized proof system giving a finite action space for derivations over simple theories in a theories folder.
why: Training a small model on checked steps rather than final programs is one way to teach a proof discipline.
caveat: The repository states it is frozen at the paper's version and the author developed a newer release elsewhere; Python and research-quality.
falsifier: Express one dawnr proof as steps in this environment; if a step needs a primitive the kernel lacks, drop it.

take: Razor builds finite models of first-order theories with a chase-inspired algorithm and reports homomorphically minimal models, with a theories directory of examples. A minimal model of a specification plus its negation gives small concrete witnesses of what a specification allows. Its README says functions and constants in its models are partial, so a term denotes an element only once the chase has created one.
why: A weak specification admits wrong outputs; minimal models enumerate small allowed behaviours without a reference solution.
caveat: Rust, first-order logic only; t specifications with arithmetic over integers fall outside a pure first-order finite-model search.
falsifier: Encode 5 weak specifications from the exploit study; if the minimal models do not include the trivial program returning nothing for the whitespace example, it does not expose weakness.

take: Take PIT's mutator catalogue as a design list for specification mutants: the boundary mutator is a table that swaps each comparison with its neighbour (less-or-equal with less-than, greater-or-equal with greater-than), alongside math, negate-conditional, increment and constant mutators. Implemented over t expressions, these give principled off-by-one and sign mutants of reference outputs.
why: A specification that accepts an off-by-one result is weak; the current gate rejects at least 60 percent of mutated outputs but with no stated mutant families to audit coverage against.
caveat: Java bytecode mutators built on ASM, so only the operator tables carry over, to be re-implemented on Python or t syntax trees; the repository also ships the Maven, Ant and HTML report modules.
code_note: ConditionalsBoundaryMethodVisitor extends AbstractJumpMutator and fills a static map from each JVM comparison opcode to a Substitution of its boundary neighbour (IFLE to IFLT, IF_ICMPGE to IF_ICMPGT and so on) with the description 'changed conditional boundary'; an opcode not in the map is simply not mutated.
falsifier: Apply the boundary, math and negation families to the reference outputs of the 232 held-out problems and score the 11 clean specifications; if the clean specifications reject every mutant of every family, the families add no information beyond the present mutation stage.

take: BLAST combines a language-model test writer with search-based test generation (Pynguin) to produce tests that reproduce an issue, keeping those that fail before and pass after. The two-component split gives a design for pairing a model's guess with a search that fills in concrete values. Its README lists RQ1 baselines, ablations and trivial instances of SWT-Bench and TDD-Bench.
why: The model often gets the structure right and misses the values; search over inputs closes that gap more cheaply than more samples.
caveat: Python repositories and the TDD-Bench benchmark; Pynguin dependency.
falsifier: Use random or search-based value generation to complete 20 model-written test skeletons; if fewer than 5 gain a failing input on a broken twin, drop it.

take: TuLiP is a Python toolbox that synthesises controllers from temporal logic specifications and can report that a specification is unrealizable. The unrealizability check is a decision procedure for whether a reactive specification can be met at all. Its README says it installs from PyPI as tulip with optional dependencies listed by a tulip.interfaces.print_env call.
why: Some wrong specifications cannot be satisfied by any program; a realizability check finds them without a model.
caveat: Temporal logic over discrete states, not integer functions; pip-installable but pulls solver dependencies.
falsifier: Run it on the reactive hysteresis specifications in the flight set; if it declares a specification realizable that is known wrong, drop it.

take: Specula has coding agents write TLA+ specifications of a system, including invariants and models of the implementation, and then checks them to find bugs; its skills directory holds the agent instructions and the root also lists case-studies and examples. The agent-writes-the-specification, model-checker-checks-it loop is the same shape as dawnr's, applied to concurrent system code.
why: Specification precision is dawnr's weak point; a published pipeline for getting an agent to produce checked invariants shows which steps they automate.
caveat: Targets concurrent and distributed system code, using TLA+ and the TLC tool chain, which dawnr does not run; its agents are commercial coding agents.
falsifier: Read the case studies and count how many bugs were found by invariants an agent wrote unaided; if fewer than half, the loop does not reliably find defects.

take: A small script that feeds the checker's error messages for a TLA+ specification back to a model with a fixed prompt kept in prompt.txt until the specification parses, with Test_Specs of broken specifications. It is the simplest instance of the checker-message repair loop whose yield dawnr has measured.
why: Self-repair from verdicts gave 2 clean of 110; a minimal published loop gives a comparison design.
caveat: Uses GPT-4, so none of its outputs may be training data; last push 2023-07.
falsifier: Run the loop shape on 20 broken t specifications with a non-excluded model; if it repairs fewer than 2 of 20, it matches dawnr's earlier rate.

take: seqax is a JAX codebase for small-to-medium LLM pretraining research whose README says the whole training program, model, optimizer and partitioning, is 500 lines. Its train.py, checkpoint I/O and input loader are a short complete reference to read against locallm's trainer for unneeded machinery.
why: locallm's training code has grown experiment by experiment; a 500-line complete baseline shows what a trainer needs.
caveat: JAX and TPU/GPU sharding rather than PyTorch; only readable as a reference; a different framework from the one dawnr's CUDA stack uses.
falsifier: List features of locallm/train.py absent from seqax and check whether any affected a measured result; if none, they are removable weight.

take: TinyLlama pretrains a 1.1B Llama on 3 trillion tokens and its repository has pretrain and sft scripts plus a small script using the Hugging Face assisted-decoding API for speculative decoding with TinyLlama as the draft model. The assisted-decoding script is a ten-minute test of draft-model speedups with any larger target.
why: dawnr ask is slow on the laptop and a small trained model could serve as a draft; this is the shortest published script for measuring that.
caveat: Archived with last push 2024-05; uses transformers' assisted generation, not llama.cpp; the models are general English models.
falsifier: Measure assisted decoding with a locallm draft and a larger target on 50 prompts; if the speedup is under 1.3 times, a draft model does not pay for itself.

take: Wanda prunes LLM weights by the product of weight magnitude and input activation norm without retraining, and the repository adds a lora_ft directory for recovering accuracy after pruning. It is the cheapest published way to try a sparse variant of the local model to cut memory.
why: Cold-start time and 6.8 GB peak memory are costs of dawnr ask; pruning plus quantisation are the two levers.
caveat: Unstructured sparsity gives no speed or memory gain in llama.cpp's dense GGUF kernels, so only structured patterns help the laptop; code last updated 2024-08.
falsifier: Prune the locallm checkpoint to 50 percent with it and compare the clean answers on 232 held-out problems; if the count falls by more than 1, pruning costs accuracy at this size.

take: The Pythia hub publishes training checkpoints and exact data order for models of several sizes, plus a predictable-memorization directory and evaluation scripts for learning dynamics. Its method for relating a training example's position in the data order to later memorization is a way to ask whether locallm answers come from rows it saw.
why: locallm's clean answers are nearly all on the 32 contaminated problems; a position-and-memorization analysis is a second test of the same claim.
caveat: Built around the Pythia models and their published data order; scripts must be adapted to locallm's own shard order, which is recorded in the token shard code.
falsifier: Correlate answer correctness with training position of the nearest source row for the 200 held-out problems; if the correlation is under 0.1, memorisation by position does not explain the pattern.

take: A nanoGPT-like research codebase from EPFL with configuration, data and optimizer packages under src and launch scripts, which the schedule and scaling paper builds on. It is a clean place to run controlled optimizer and schedule ablations at small scale.
why: Learning-rate and width experiments exist in locallm (exp_lr_width.py); a published baseline repository enables cross-checking the setup.
caveat: Uses web-text datasets; code uses distributed-friendly wrappers; no code data.
falsifier: Reproduce one locallm learning-rate sweep in it; if the best learning rate differs by more than a factor of 2, one setup has a bug.

take: SparseGPT prunes and quantises a transformer layer by layer with a one-shot second-order update; sparsegpt.py and quant.py are the layer-wise solver and the quantiser. They are reference code for post-training compression with a calibration set.
why: The existing int8 path has no calibration-based method; this is a reference for adding one.
caveat: Written for OPT, BLOOM and LLaMA modules; locallm's layers would need adapter code.
falsifier: Quantise one locallm layer with it and with round-to-nearest; if the layer's output error is not at least 20 percent lower, calibration does not help at this size.

take: pi-vcc compacts a long agent conversation without any model call: build-sections.ts assembles structured sections from the transcript, filter-noise.ts drops low-value output, and drill-down.ts lets the agent ask for the full text of one numbered item later. A drill-down index makes compaction lossless for a small model whose own summaries are unreliable.
why: A small local model summarises poorly, and context management for the repository assistant must not depend on it.
caveat: TypeScript for the Pi agent host; only the extraction rules and the numbered-reference idea transfer to Python; benchmarks are the project's own.
falsifier: Compact 30 recorded assistant sessions this way and replay their last question; if answer correctness falls by more than 2 of 30, compaction loses needed text.

take: code-review-graph builds a local tree-sitter knowledge graph of a repository, serves it over MCP and the command line, and includes a changes module for which files a change touches and a context_savings module that reports how much context was avoided. Both modules are Python and show how a change-aware retrieval step can be measured.
why: The assistant's retrieval is judged by recall; a change-aware graph and a context-saved measure give a second view.
caveat: Requires Python 3.10 or later and tree-sitter packages with native wheels; the star count and benchmark claims are the project's own; modules were listed, not read.
falsifier: Run the graph's change analysis on 30 commits from the repository and check the touched files against git; if it misses more than 3 of 30, the graph is not reliable.

take: An MCP server written in C that indexes code, documentation and configuration into a persistent local graph and offers change-aware test selection, with install scripts for Linux, macOS and Windows (install.sh and install.ps1). It shows a native-code indexer that starts quickly, relevant to the cold-start cost.
why: dawnr ask takes 64.6 s from a cold start; a native indexer is a candidate for the part that scans the repository.
caveat: Large C project with vendored dependencies; MCP server rather than a library; claims not verified.
falsifier: Time its index build against the Python index on the repository; if it is less than 5 times faster, startup is not dominated by indexing.

take: A TypeScript tool that pre-indexes a codebase into a graph, keeps it synced on file changes and serves it to coding agents, with a codegraph-kernel directory. The sync-on-change design is the reference for incremental re-indexing.
why: Re-indexing the whole repository after each edit is wasteful on a laptop; incremental sync keeps the cache warm.
caveat: The tree contains a TELEMETRY.md and telemetry directories, so any reuse must strip them; installs through npm.
falsifier: Edit one file in a 1,000-file repository and compare re-index time with a full build; if incremental is not at least 10 times faster, drop it.

take: PatchAgent is a language-model program repair agent from USENIX Security 2025 whose repository is a production fork for real-world bug fixing, with a Dockerfile and docker-compose set-up. It is a reference for an agent that reads a failing report, edits and re-runs, which is what a witness-fed repair round tries to do for specifications.
why: One witness-fed repair round moved few cells; a published agent design shows what extra tools a repairer gets.
caveat: Needs a model and a Docker set-up; the research artifact lives in a separate repository; code was not read.
falsifier: Compare its tool set with the repair round's inputs; if every tool it uses is already provided, the design adds nothing.

take: Sorald repairs violations of 25+ SonarQube static-analysis rules in Java by deterministic, template-based source transformations rather than a model, with a HANDLED_RULES list. Rule-to-fix templates are a model-free source of candidate repairs for diagnostics that have a standard fix.
why: The missing ingredient in repair is a candidate; rules with fixed fixes supply candidates at no model cost.
caveat: Java and SonarQube specific; dawnr would need its own diagnostic-to-fix table.
falsifier: Write fix templates for the 5 most frequent lowering diagnostics; if they repair fewer than 10 percent of failures, templates are too narrow.

take: A minimal GRPO implementation of about three files, aimed at training a small Llama locally on one node with a loss module and a replay buffer. Reading it before using a larger framework shows the entire policy-gradient update with group-relative advantages in one sitting.
why: Training against a verifier on one card needs the update rule understood, not hidden in a framework.
caveat: README targets a 3B model and a conda environment with Python 3.12; the reward is a toy; last push 2025-01.
falsifier: Replace its reward with test-pass on 50 training problems; if the mean reward does not rise over 100 steps, the setup does not learn.

take: Cerberus wraps many analysis and repair tools and benchmark suites behind one interface; its benchmark directory lists entries (git submodules) for C bug collections including ExtractFix, ManyBugs, a vulnerability track and a functional track of the APR competition. They name real C defects with known fixes, which are the test set for how often the native gate finds a real bug.
why: The gate has found few real defects and has no recall measure; defects with known fixes allow one.
caveat: Python orchestration around Docker images per benchmark; most defects are in whole programs and need function extraction; the loader directories hold scripts, not the data itself.
falsifier: Select 15 defects in functions with at most 64-bit inputs and run the gate; if it finds fewer than 5 of 15 known defects, recall is below one third and that is the number to improve.

take: A collection of Semgrep rules for vulnerability research in C, where each rule in rules/c has a matching .c file of vulnerable and safe samples (double-free, command-injection and about fifty more). Running them over an open-source C project shortlists functions worth turning into a native case, and the paired samples show what each pattern looks like.
why: The finding-to-case cost is the bottleneck on real bugs; a cheap pre-filter chooses where to spend authoring effort.
caveat: Semgrep is a separate program installed with pip or binaries; the rules aim at security bug classes, not arithmetic errors in numeric code; hits are leads, not defects.
falsifier: Run the rules over a pinned C project and write cases for the first 10 hits; if the gate confirms fewer than 2 of 10, the rules are a poor shortlist.

take: goSAT is an SMT solver for floating-point arithmetic that casts satisfiability to a global optimisation problem, with src and tools directories. It is an independent way to look for binary32 inputs that violate a property, beside CBMC's bit-blasted floating-point.
why: Flight checks use binary64 where production uses binary32; a floating-point-native solver searches the binary32 space directly.
caveat: Last push 2018-01; incomplete (optimisation can miss solutions) and builds against old Z3; found only by README and tree.
falsifier: Ask it for an input where a binary32 hysteresis function differs from its binary64 version; if it finds none that sampling did not find, it adds nothing.

take: dReal is a delta-complete SMT solver for nonlinear real arithmetic including trigonometric functions. It can bound the real-number behaviour of quaternion and angle functions in flight code, to compare with sampled binary32 results.
why: Rounding error claims need a real-number reference; a delta-complete solver gives answers for sin and cos that bit-blasting cannot.
caveat: C++ with Bazel or CMake builds, Linux and macOS; answers are delta-satisfiable, not exact.
falsifier: Bound the quaternion norm after one integration step with it; if it cannot decide the property at delta 1e-6 in 10 minutes, it is too slow for this use.

take: libdiffuzz is a custom memory allocator that fills fresh allocations with different bytes on each run so reads from uninitialised memory change the output, with src holding the allocator. The trick, running twice with different fill and comparing, is a cheap native replay check for uninitialised reads that ASan does not report.
why: Native replay runs under UBSan and ASan, neither of which flags uninitialised reads (MSan does but is not always available).
caveat: Rust crate for Rust programs, last push 2020; only the idea applies to C replays.
falsifier: Run 10 replays twice with different malloc fill bytes; if none produces differing output on a known uninitialised-read case, the check does not work.

take: Use json_repair as the tolerant reader in front of the Cohere JSON path: a recursive-descent parser (parse_object, parse_array, parse_string, parse_number, parse_comment) that fixes missing quotes, trailing commas and truncated output, with a logging option that returns the list of repairs and a strict mode that disables the guessing. It supplies the baseline for how many of the 500 replies a generic repairer converts compared with the 142 JSON-v2 converted.
why: JSON-v2 converted 142 of 500 replies but kept 2 strict problems; a repair library shows whether the loss is at parsing or at the content that remains after parsing.
caveat: Python package with no dependencies; its heuristics can invent content (it can turn a truncated string into a valid but wrong one), so repaired replies must pass the strict static, round-trip and reference checks unchanged and the repair log kept as evidence.
code_note: json_parser.py's JSONParser takes logging, stream_stable and strict flags; a comment in the constructor says strict mode was added to disable some of the repair heuristics; the parse_* methods are split into files per JSON type, and when logging is on each repair is recorded with its context instead of being applied silently.
falsifier: Run it on the 500 recorded Cohere replies and count those that parse and pass the strict checks; if it converts fewer than the 142 already converted, or its additional conversions add 0 strict problems, repair is not the lever.

take: Sibila extracts typed data into Pydantic objects or dataclasses from local or remote models, and for local llama.cpp models it converts a JSON schema into a grammar (json_schema.py, json_grammar.py) before generation. The conversion from a Python type to a schema to a grammar is the path a signature-derived constraint would take on the GGUF model.
why: The local model runs on llama.cpp, whose structured mode is a grammar; the type-and-scope restriction must be compiled to one.
caveat: Last push 2024-06 and uses llama-cpp-python; the grammar generator covers JSON only, not t's syntax; the library also targets many hosted APIs that are irrelevant.
falsifier: Compile 20 signature schemas to grammars through its path and sample with the local model; if more than 2 of 20 grammars are rejected by llama.cpp, the path needs rewriting.

take: A single-binary GGUF engine in C that serves, scores and fine-tunes LoRA through quantized weights, with CPU, CUDA and Metal back ends, an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API, and a README promise of answering 'will it fit' and 'why is my laptop out of memory'. The memory-fit estimation is the part to compare with llama.cpp.
why: dawnr ask peaks at 6.8 GB on the laptop; a predictor of fit and memory would explain where the peak comes from.
caveat: 30 stars, new project, claims signed receipts and byte-reproducibility that were not checked; replaces rather than complements llama.cpp.
falsifier: Compare its predicted memory for the local model with the measured 6.8 GB peak; if it is off by more than 15 percent, drop it.

take: BlendSQL is a query language that blends SQL with local language-model calls, constraining the model's outputs to the types and values in the database. Restricting a model's choice to values present in a table is the same idea as restricting names to those in scope.
why: In-scope names are an enumerated set per problem; constraining a model to choose among given values is the simplest instance.
caveat: Targets SQL tables and its own dialect; the constraint mechanism sits on libraries (guidance, outlines) that dawnr already knows.
falsifier: Constrain a model to choose a variable name from the in-scope list for 50 holes; if the chosen name is wrong in more than 10, enumeration alone is not enough.

take: Study the layer-streaming planner and runtime: the frozen base weights live in CPU RAM and are streamed one decoder layer at a time into a small pool of pre-allocated GPU buffers, so peak VRAM is one layer plus one vocabulary matrix while only LoRA adapters, their gradients and optimizer state stay resident. A planner module forecasts VRAM and throughput before a run starts.
why: Training budget is limited and one RTX 4080 has 16 GB; streaming makes LoRA fine-tuning of a base larger than the card possible, and the forecast avoids wasted runs.
caveat: Marked BETA in its own module docstring (v0.72.0); an architecture allowlist limits which models stream; throughput is bounded by PCIe, so a 4080 will train slowly; a very large package whose YAML front end is not needed; the stars and website claims were not verified.
code_note: layer_stream.py is documented as the pure half (tier choice, pinned versus pageable memory decision, architecture allowlist, VRAM and throughput arithmetic) with no top-level torch import so the light CLI can forecast without the training stack; the runtime half (buffer pool, weight source, prefetch scheduler, layer wrapper) is in layer_stream_runtime.py, and bounds on buffers and read-ahead are imported from a dependency-free module.
falsifier: LoRA-tune a 7B-class base on the RTX 4080 with it and with the standard 4-bit path; if the streamed run is more than 3 times slower per step with no gain in held-out clean answers on the 232 problems, it does not help.

take: GraphGen builds a knowledge graph from source text and uses it to generate supervised fine-tuning question-answer data with coverage of the graph's under-covered parts. The idea of generating data to fill measured coverage gaps is the model for choosing which t constructs a teacher should be asked about.
why: Teacher recipes add zero rows when they repeat covered problems; targeting uncovered parts of the space is the corrective.
caveat: Generation uses a language model whose output may fall under dawnr's rule on model-written data; method only.
falsifier: Apply coverage-gap selection to the frozen 50 uncovered training problems; if the selection picks fewer than 10 that the current selection misses, it adds nothing.

take: KitOps packages models, datasets and code with their metadata into a versioned artifact in an OCI registry, described in a Kitfile. The Kitfile idea, one manifest naming the weights, data and code of a result, is a reference for the receipts attached to releases.
why: Every claim should link to inputs by hash; a standard manifest format avoids inventing one.
caveat: Go program tied to OCI registries; overkill for a public repository release.
falsifier: Write the manifest for one finished run; if more than 3 fields cannot be filled from the existing run record, the record is incomplete.

take: CPR repairs C programs with concolic execution over an abstract patch, a patch with symbolic parameters, and refines the abstraction as test paths are explored, with the stated goal of over-fitting the initial tests less. Over-fitting to the tests is the repair analogue of a specification that passes its own checks but is wrong.
why: A repair accepted by tests only can be a wrong function that fits the examples; refinement against explored paths reduces that.
caveat: Last push 2022-10; Python driver around KLEE-style concolic execution in Docker; written for C repair benchmarks, not for specifications.
falsifier: Run it on 5 of the fixed PX4 defects; if the repair it returns equals the upstream fix in fewer than 2 of 5, it does not help.

take: FixMorph transfers a fix (patch) from one version of a C program to another, syntactically similar version, for software that maintains several versions such as the Linux kernel. When the gate finds a defect in a pinned old version, it is a way to produce the corresponding fix for the current upstream head.
why: Upstream pull requests from findings need the fix on the current version, while cases are pinned to an older commit.
caveat: Python orchestrating clang-based tools in Docker images for Ubuntu 16.04 and 20.04, so it will not run natively on the three platforms without a container.
falsifier: Port 3 existing fixes from pinned to head versions; if fewer than 2 apply and compile, it is not a time saver.

take: The core package chunks code by syntax tree with an ast-splitter and falls back to a text splitter built on LangChain's, and the repository has an evaluation directory comparing retrieval with and without the index. The two-splitter structure shows how to keep chunking robust when a grammar fails.
why: Chunking is the cheapest retrieval improvement and a syntax-aware splitter needs a fallback for files that do not parse.
caveat: TypeScript in a pnpm workspace with a Python directory; the main use is as an MCP server backed by a hosted vector database, which dawnr would not use.
falsifier: Port the fallback rule and measure recall at 10 on the retrieval set with and without it; if unparsable files make up under 1 percent of the corpus, the fallback is unnecessary.

take: Lift the stand-in discipline of a firmware project that runs CBMC in CI: per-library fake_host/cbmc_*.c files compiled under #ifdef CBMC, where functions a proof must never reach call ASSERT(false, name) so reaching one is a finding, harmless hardware queries return constants (a 32-bit physical-address width), and a compare_summary.py script fails the build when a baseline coverage or failed-assert count gets worse. These are the libc-model and regression-gate pieces the native gate hand-writes per case.
why: CBMC gives no usable snprintf or ctype bodies and stand-ins are hand-written; a convention of unreachable-by-assertion stubs makes an unmodelled call visible instead of silently unconstrained.
caveat: Specific to the RMM firmware's build system (CMake, tb_common.h, ASSERT macro) and its Arm-specific headers; BSD-3-Clause for the project but third-party directories may carry other licences; the summary format parsed by compare_summary.py is CBMC-viewer-like text, not the JSON the native gate uses.
code_note: cbmc_xlat_low_va.c implements xlat_low_va_setup and xlat_low_va_mmu_cfg as ASSERT(false, name) so any proof that calls them fails, and the rest as parameter-ignoring no-ops returning 0; compare_summary.py parses a summary table, logs 'CBMC Analysis failed' for rows whose result is N/A, and compares coverage and failed-assert counts against a baseline, reporting when the count of failed asserts increased.
falsifier: Replace the hand-written stand-ins of 5 existing native cases with assert-false stubs for functions the harness should not reach; if a previously passing case now fails because it reaches an unmodelled call, the convention has exposed a silent gap, and if none changes the convention adds nothing.

take: Triton is a dynamic binary analysis library with dynamic symbolic execution, taint analysis, an AST representation of semantics and Python bindings. Given a compiled native replay binary and a CBMC witness, it can symbolically explore neighbouring paths to produce more inputs for the same defect.
why: A single witness is replayed; sibling inputs on the same path are what a person needs to write a minimal reproducing case.
caveat: C++ library with Python bindings built with CMake and vcpkg; x86 and ARM binary support; heavy install on Windows.
falsifier: Run it on the replay binary of 3 cases; if it finds no new input beyond the CBMC witnesses within 10 minutes each, it adds nothing.

take: Gillian is an OCaml platform for compositional symbolic execution and verification, instantiated for C (Gillian-C, over CompCert-C), JavaScript and a teaching language. It is a separation-logic-based checker for C pointer code to run beside CBMC on cases with heap structures.
why: Heap and pointer cases are where the gate's hand-built scalar inputs are weakest.
caveat: Works on CompCert-C syntax after compilation with CompCert, which adds a licensing and build step; OCaml toolchain.
falsifier: Verify one list or buffer function; if it needs more than 20 lines of specification for a function CBMC handles in a harness, the burden is too high.

take: Use Darum's approach to brittle verification: run Dafny repeatedly with random seeds, collect each symbol's resource count, compare the distributions across runs and report extremes, with a resource-count limit (default 10M) and an option to isolate assertions. It turns 'the proof is unstable' into a per-symbol number, for Dafny, one of the seven kernels.
why: Proof results can be unstable and a timeout is not a verdict; measured resource variance tells which cells' pass or fail depends on the seed.
caveat: Dafny only; a Poetry project written against Dafny's resource-count output formats of 2025, so output parsing must be checked against the pinned Dafny version; zero stars and a single maintainer.
code_note: dafny_measure.py parses arguments for the Dafny executable, a random seed (time-seeded by default), the number of mutations (10), a symbol filter, the resource-count limit as a magnitude with K, M or G suffix, and an output directory; the other modules read the logs, plot distributions and find the extreme runs.
falsifier: Run 10 seeded repeats on the Dafny lowering of the 213 verified programs; if no program's resource count varies by more than 2 times between seeds, instability is not present in Dafny cells at this size.

take: Lift the k-induction wrapper around CBMC: the base step runs cbmc with an unwindset of main.X at k and no unwinding assertions, and the induction step rewrites the C file with a pycparser-based transformer that havocs the variables of the main loop before it, using SV-COMP havoc functions inserted ahead of the loop. It removes the hand-chosen loop bound for one-loop programs.
why: Loops are bounded by hand and a bound hides defects beyond it; k-induction turns a bounded pass into an unbounded proof when it succeeds.
caveat: Limited by its own README to one-loop embedded-style C programs; last push 2020-02, written for an older CBMC command-line; a Python 3 tool with a slicing and variable-moving module.
code_note: kinduction.py defines VERIFIER_BASE_CALL and VERIFIER_INDUCTION_CALL as cbmc.sh invocations with --unwindset main.X:KINCREMENT --no-unwinding-assertions, installs a signal handler, and prepare_induction_step de-anonymises aggregates, parses the code, builds a havoc block from declarations and inserts it before the main loop; the base step needs no change to the file.
falsifier: Apply it to 3 existing cases that have a single loop and compare with their hand unwinding on CBMC 6.11; if k-induction does not prove them at k up to 10, or contradicts the bounded verdict, it does not help.

take: Lift the order of repair attempts in verus_solver: the verifier's errors are parsed into classes, a triage step picks the top error class by a configured strategy order, a deterministic patch engine applies fixes first, and only when it cannot does a language-model fallback run. It sits beside the AutoVerus and VeruSAGE systems and benchmarks in the same repository.
why: A model-first repair round moved the gate from 66 to 69 of 182; deterministic patches for common error classes cost no model call and leave the model to the rest.
caveat: Specific to Verus's error messages and Rust source; the repository includes a directory of results from a GPT-5 run, which may be read as a benchmark but never used as training data; one maintainer and no stars.
code_note: triage.py's top_error_class(result, strategy_order) returns the first error class found in the verifier result following the strategy order; the package splits parsing (error_parser.py), deterministic fixing (patch_engine.py), model use (llm_fallback.py), checkpointing (checkpoint.py) and scoring (scorer.py) into separate modules.
falsifier: Classify the failures of the 182 cells by error class using such a parser; if fewer than 20 percent fall in classes with a deterministic fix, the patch-first order does not apply to dawnr's failures.

take: COCONUT-SVSM keeps Verus-verified modules as .verus.rs files beside the ordinary Rust (address, address space, allocator) and a top-level verification directory. The split between production source and verified models is a worked example of verification in a real kernel project and of Verus at tens of files.
why: Verus lowering failures give little feedback; real Verus code in a maintained project shows the patterns that pass in practice.
caveat: Rust no_std kernel code needing a pinned toolchain and the Verus fork; the .verus.rs convention is the project's own.
falsifier: Run Verus on three of its modules and record verification time; if any takes over 120 seconds, large real modules are beyond the budget dawnr gives each cell.

take: Read the function contracts written as C macros in poly.c: requires, ensures, assigns, memory_no_alias, array_abs_bound and loop decreases clauses on scalar and small-array arithmetic such as Barrett reduction, whose CBMC harness has only an int16_t input and checks the contract with CHECK_FUNCTION_CONTRACTS. They are a model of the scalar-input, bounded-output cases the native gate prefers, with contracts that CBMC checks and then assumes at call sites.
why: Native cases take scalar inputs of at most 64 bits; contracts on such arithmetic functions are a supply of ready case descriptions with expected postconditions.
caveat: The LICENSE says all source in mlkem/* and dev/* is under a choice of Apache-2.0, ISC or MIT, while files outside the library, including the harnesses under proofs/cbmc, state their own SPDX identifiers (the harness read carries MIT-0 AND Apache-2.0), so only mlkem/ is listed as taken and harness text must not be copied without checking each header; the contract macros need CBMC's contract front end.
license_quote: of the Apache-2.0 license OR the ISC license OR the MIT license
code_note: poly.c wraps contracts in __contract__(...) with requires(b > -MLKEM_Q_HALF && b < MLKEM_Q_HALF) and ensures(return_value > -MLKEM_Q && return_value < MLKEM_Q) on a scalar reduction, assigns(memory_slice(r, sizeof(mlk_poly))) and array_abs_bound on a polynomial routine, and decreases(MLKEM_N - i) on loops; in the harness the call is the only statement after declaring unconstrained int16_t inputs.
falsifier: Write native cases for 5 of its scalar reductions from their contracts and check original versus a one-line mutation of each; if CBMC 6.11 does not refute at least 4 of the 5 mutants, the contracts do not make good case descriptions.

take: Use casa's samplers for grammar-constrained sampling that does not distort the model's distribution: CARS (constrained adaptive rejection sampling, with max_attempts defaulting to 100), rejection, MCMC and GCD variants, with grammar recognizers built on llguidance or xgrammar. It supports a comparison between hard-masked decoding and distribution-preserving sampling at equal sample budgets.
why: Answer rate may be a search budget before it is a training problem, and hard constraints can change which answers a small model prefers; this library allows measuring both.
caveat: Requires Python 3.12 or later and a CUDA GPU per its README, a young research package (8 stars, 2026-07); samplers operate on Hugging Face models rather than llama.cpp; attempts that exhaust the budget return fewer samples than asked.
code_note: CARS.sample(prompt, n_samples, max_attempts=100) delegates to a _GenerateCARS routine in rejection.py that loops up to max_attempts, with timeout variants selected by a flag; the grammar recognizers wrap llguidance and xgrammar behind the same interface, and an oracle trie caches constrained probabilities.
falsifier: Sample 10 answers per problem on the 232 held-out problems with CARS and with hard-masked decoding; if the count of problems with at least one clean answer does not differ by 2 or more, distribution distortion is not the limit.

take: This implements the ASAp algorithm of Grammar-Aligned Decoding, which adaptively corrects the sampling distribution of grammar-constrained decoding so that the constrained output is drawn in proportion to the model's own probabilities rather than distorted by masking. The correction is the missing piece when the constrained model is judged on rate of clean answers.
why: Constrained decoding earlier doubled parsing but gave only 1.23 times more passing tests; a distortion of the model's preferences is one stated reason.
caveat: Research code for Hugging Face transformers, last push 2025-02, with examples for specific grammars; the NeurIPS 2024 claims are the authors'.
falsifier: Run it on the t grammar for 100 problems and compare the test pass rate with plain masking; if the pass rate differs by under 1 percentage point, the distortion does not matter here.

take: DiverseGuide steers structured generation with automata to produce different valid outputs across samples, an artifact for an ICFEM 2026 paper with regex_dfa_guide and a native directory. It is a way to spread samples over distinct valid programs when drawing many answers per problem.
why: With a verifier choosing the winner, more diverse samples raise pass@k; masked decoding tends to repeat the same valid shape.
caveat: Zero stars and brand new; Dockerfile and a reproducibility document; regex and DFA based, so the context-free parts of t would need a different guide.
