falsifier: Draw 8 samples per problem with and without it; if the number of distinct verified programs among 8 does not rise by 20 percent, diversity steering does not help.

take: StrataPython translates Python programs into Strata's intermediate representations, Core and Laurel, for formal verification, written in Lean 4 and built with lake build; it generates the Python AST types and has compile-time tests. It is a recent example of lowering Python (the language of dawnr's reference solutions) into a verifier IR rather than directly to a prover.
why: An intermediate verification representation shared by several back ends addresses the problem that seven lowerings each re-implement semantics.
caveat: Three stars, a very recent project, and the Strata IR itself is a separate dependency; the translation covers a subset of Python.
falsifier: Translate 20 reference solutions with it; if fewer than 10 translate, the covered subset is too small.

take: VERT's artifact checks a language-model transpilation to Rust against a reference by running a bolero property test and a bounded Kani proof of equivalence with timeouts from config.py (bolero_timeout, all_timeout), and torust.py extracts parameter bounds from argument types to bound the check. Differential checking of a produced program against a trusted one is the pattern for validating a lowering of t.
why: No lowering of t has a check that the lowered program means the same as the source; running both on bounded inputs with a proof tool is a design for one.
caveat: Setup pins Rust, Clang, a fork of cargo-bolero and Kani 0.55.0; the README's generation step calls hosted models (the code imports a Claude client), so generated outputs must not be used as training data; zero stars and an artifact-style layout.
falsifier: Apply the bounded-equivalence idea to the Python interpreter versus the Dafny lowering on 30 programs; if it finds a disagreement that the existing matrix did not, the lowerings were not validated by the matrix alone.

take: SpaceWasm is NASA JPL's WebAssembly interpreter for on-board use, the interpreter behind F Prime's WasmSequencer, with fuzz and tests directories in a Rust workspace. It is an example of flight software developed with fuzzing, which sets a reference for evidence a flight function should carry.
why: Flight-domain evidence in dawnr is bounded comparisons; a flight-compliant project shows what testing artefacts accompany real flight code.
caveat: Rust, not C or C++; the relevant directories were listed only; an AI_POLICY.md is listed at the root and its content was not read, but it must be read before any upstream pull request.
falsifier: Count fuzz targets per module; if fewer than 3 of its modules have fuzz targets, the evidence standard is lower than assumed.

take: Take MCY's pipeline for judging whether checks are strong: generate thousands of mutations of a design, filter them with formal verification so that only mutations that can change the design's output remain, run the testbench against those, and report which relevant mutants no check detects. The formal filter that discards equivalent mutants is the step the specification mutation stage lacks.
why: A specification that accepts a mutated output may have caught nothing because the mutant is equivalent to the original; filtering equivalents first makes the reject rate of 60 percent meaningful.
caveat: Hardware designs in Yosys netlists, driven by a click-based Python CLI that stores mutations and results in sqlite; ISC licence; the idea carries over, not the netlist handling.
code_note: mcy.py is a click command-line program with coloured log helpers, an sqlite3 connection helper that can require an existing database, a xorshift32 generator for reproducible mutation selection, and a configuration reader that checks which mutate options are set; errors exit through exit_mcy with a return code and a forced shutdown handler for signals.
falsifier: For the 232 reference solutions, drop mutants that agree with the original on 10,000 random inputs and re-score the specification stage; if the reject rate over the remaining non-equivalent mutants differs from the present 60 percent threshold result by under 5 points, the filter changes nothing.

take: CastXML outputs an XML description of the abstract syntax tree of C and C++ declarations using the Clang front end. It gives exact function signatures, parameter types and class membership for headers, the information needed to generate harness stubs and to find which C++ functions have scalar-only signatures.
why: A C++ function has no case at all, and signatures of overloaded or class members cannot be recovered by pattern matching.
caveat: Needs a Clang installation and CMake build per platform; outputs declarations, not bodies, so function text must still be extracted separately.
falsifier: Extract signatures of 50 PX4 C++ functions and count those with only scalar parameters; if fewer than 5, scalar-input C++ cases are rare and the effort is not justified.

take: CMock generates mock and stub functions for C headers, with a Ruby generator in lib, a small runtime in src and a configuration directory for what to stub. Generated stubs for a function's callees are the starting point for a harness whose callees CBMC cannot model.
why: Harness stand-ins are hand-written; a stub generator removes the typing for callee declarations.
caveat: A Ruby project (Gemfile and gemspec in the tree) built around the Unity test framework; its mocks are made for unit tests, whereas CBMC stubs need nondeterministic returns.
falsifier: Generate stubs for the callees of 5 existing cases and modify them to return nondeterministic values; if that takes longer than writing them by hand, drop it.

take: Cifra is a collection of cryptographic primitives for embedded use, with clarity and simplicity as its first aim, in plain C. Its small block, hash and curve functions are candidates for native cases with array inputs of fixed size.
why: Native cases need open-source C with bounded loops and fixed-size buffers; embedded-style crypto fits and has published test vectors to check cases against.
caveat: Released as CC0-1.0; last push 2023-10; the README states clarity as its first aim, so the code is meant to be read.
falsifier: Write cases for 5 functions and check with the published test vectors; if CBMC cannot reach a complete verdict for at least 3 at 8-byte or smaller bounds, the loops are too deep for the gate.

take: cJSON is an ANSI C JSON parser and printer in one source file with a tests directory. Its number parsing and printing, buffer growth and string escape handling are string-to-scalar functions of the kind used to look for defects, and its git history can be searched for fixed defects.
why: The gate needs real C functions with a known bug history to measure recall.
caveat: Allocation is likely to go through the library's own allocator functions, so cases may need an allocation stand-in (not checked); MIT; one source file of several thousand lines.
falsifier: Write cases for 5 functions with fixed historical defects at the commit before the fix; if the gate finds fewer than 2 of 5, recall on real parser bugs is low.

take: ctypesgen is a pure-Python wrapper generator that reads C headers and produces ctypes bindings. The bindings allow calling a compiled C function directly from Python on thousands of inputs, for differential testing of the C function against its Python reference solution.
why: Replay compiles a new C binary per case; a loadable library called from Python makes large input sweeps cheap.
caveat: Parses headers with its own preprocessor handling, which fails on complex macros; callers must compile the library themselves.
falsifier: Sweep 100,000 inputs through a compiled PX4 function and its Python port; if the sweep takes longer than compiling and running the replay binary, drop it.

take: Dion's repository carries a plain reference Muon (muon_reference.py), a NorMuon variant and a Triton Newton-Schulz kernel beside its distributed Dion optimizers. For a single card the reference file and the Triton kernel show the orthogonalisation step both as readable code and as a fused GPU kernel.
why: If Muon helps at locallm size, the Newton-Schulz step is the only extra cost per step; a fused kernel decides whether that cost is negligible on an RTX 4080.
caveat: Triton kernels need Linux or WSL with a supported Triton build; the distributed parts are not needed on one card; the README tells users to prefer Dion2 or Dion3 over the legacy Dion.
falsifier: Time the reference and the Triton Newton-Schulz on the model's weight shapes on the 4080; if the extra time per optimizer step exceeds 10 percent, the cost is not negligible.

take: PowerInfer is a llama.cpp-derived engine that, per its README, leverages activation locality to serve large models on a consumer GPU, with a converter producing its own GGUF variant (convert-hf-to-powerinfer-gguf.py) and a powerinfer-py package for the predictor. It is the published attempt to run models larger than VRAM on one consumer card.
why: The local card is one RTX 4080; offloading by activation sparsity is an alternative to layer streaming for running a larger model at inference.
caveat: A fork of an older llama.cpp (the tree has atomic_windows.h and Metal/CUDA/OpenCL backends but its own GGUF variant), so it is unlikely to be combinable with a current llama.cpp; which models it supports was not checked.
falsifier: Run the engine's smallest supported model on the 4080 against current llama.cpp with the same quantisation; if tokens per second is not at least 1.3 times higher, drop it.

take: OctoPack builds instruction data from git commits, where the commit message is the instruction and the diff gives the before-and-after code, with dataset, finetuning and evaluation directories. Commits that fix defects are human-written (before, after) repair pairs, unlike model-written teacher data.
why: Repair rows currently come from visible-test failures; commit history supplies fixes with human intent and no model involvement.
caveat: The commit data is mostly general code; the extracted pairs would need filtering to defect-fixing commits in C and Python; dataset directory contents were not opened.
falsifier: Extract fix commits for the C projects used in the native gate; if fewer than 100 yield compilable before-and-after functions, it is too small to train on.

take: ONNX Runtime GenAI implements the generation loop for ONNX models on device, including logits processing, and its tree has Windows build files (build.bat, generate_dml_shaders.bat) beside Linux scripts. It is a cross-platform alternative runtime to measure start-up time and memory against llama.cpp.
why: dawnr ask takes 64.6 s cold with a 6.8 GB peak on the laptop; a different runtime with its own loader may start faster.
caveat: Needs the model exported to ONNX, a step locallm lacks; the benchmark directory was only listed.
falsifier: Export the local model and measure cold start and peak memory; if either is not at least 20 percent better than llama.cpp's, drop it.

take: Take the commit analyzer from the AIxCC challenge-project template that Atlantis builds on: parse_repo.py walks a project's git history with a CommitParser and a ProjectParser and records, per commit, the files and the names of functions whose bodies changed, ignoring changes outside function scope. For C projects that yields the function-level before-and-after pairs of every fix commit, the raw material for choosing real cases.
why: The finding-to-case cost is the bottleneck on real bugs; a list of functions changed by fix commits points straight at functions whose pinned pre-fix version is the original case source.
caveat: The repository is Team Atlanta's semifinal submission with a MIT licence at the root and a MIT licence file in crs-cp-user from the competition organisers; the repository also has a proprietary directory that was not taken; the template expects projects laid out as src/<subdir> with a project definition file; the final-round system by the same team is GPL-3.0 and not used; the src directory also holds model-calling files (LLMManager.py, chat.py) that are not part of the take.
code_note: parse_repo iterates the (subdir, ref) pairs a ProjectParser reports, runs CommitParser(...).parse_repo(analyze_unit='commit'), and for each commit change collects the after_file and function_name of every function change into per-commit file and function lists in a nested defaultdict; its docstring states that changes outside function scope such as structure definitions and globals are not considered.
falsifier: Run it on the git history of a pinned C project and keep commits whose message names a fix; if fewer than 20 percent of those yield a changed function with only scalar parameters, it yields too few usable cases.

take: RepoGraph builds a repository-level code graph of definitions and references with construct_graph.py and retrieves the subgraph around a target line with graph_searcher.py, plugged into the SWE-agent and Agentless pipelines. The k-hop neighbourhood retrieval is a code-aware alternative to text similarity for supplying context to a small model.
why: Dense retrieval returns similar text; a definition-and-reference graph returns what a function actually uses.
caveat: Python; its requirements.txt was not read; built around SWE-bench-style tasks; last push 2025-04.
falsifier: Compare graph-neighbourhood context with top-5 text retrieval on 50 repository questions; if answer correctness does not rise by 3 answers of 50, drop it.

take: Monty is a Python interpreter written in Rust that runs code written by a model inside a sandbox started in under a millisecond from a pool, according to its README, instead of a container taking about 1500 ms. It could run the model-written Python reference solutions and tests of the teacher pipeline without a container.
why: Teacher and assistant pipelines execute untrusted Python many times; per-run container start-up is a cost and a platform dependency.
caveat: It implements a subset of Python, with a limitations page in the tree, so tests using unsupported libraries fail; the README separates the MIT OSS Monty from a commercial server, which is not taken.
falsifier: Run the 232 reference solutions and their tests under it; if more than 10 percent fail for unsupported features, the subset is too small for the pipeline.

take: LEANN is a vector index for personal devices whose README claims 97 percent less storage than conventional indexes without accuracy loss and that it tracks no telemetry, with packages, benchmarks and apps directories. A much smaller index is what matters for the laptop; how it achieves that is described in the paper it links, which was not read.
why: Peak memory is 6.8 GB and disk and load time count toward the cold start; a smaller index loads faster.
caveat: The savings claim is the project's own and not verified; any query-time cost was not checked; it has a .gitmodules file and a docker directory.
falsifier: Build both indexes over the repository corpus and compare size, query latency and recall at 10; if recall falls by more than 1 point or query latency rises more than 3 times, it does not help.

take: Microsandbox runs untrusted workloads in local microVMs with hardware isolation, fork and snapshot of live sandboxes, OCI image support, and, per its README, support on Linux, macOS and Windows, with SDKs. It is the only sandbox in this list claiming all three of dawnr's platforms with hardware isolation.
why: The repository assistant runs model-chosen shell commands and builds on three platforms; OS-level policies differ, a microVM does not.
caveat: Rust runtime with vendored dependencies and a requirement for virtualisation support (not checked on the laptop); README claims about startup time are the project's; heavier than a policy sandbox.
falsifier: Run the build and test commands of one repository in it on the Windows laptop; if start-up takes more than 5 seconds or the build is more than 1.5 times slower than native, it is too heavy.

take: The author's repository for Muon holds muon_update, a pure function on gradient and momentum buffers with beta 0.95, five Newton-Schulz steps and Nesterov momentum that flattens four-dimensional convolution filters, and an optimizer class with lr 0.02 and AdamW-style weight decay that shards parameters across ranks. Its stand-alone muon_update can be called from locallm's existing optimizer loop on 2-D weight matrices.
why: Optimizer choice is a cheap variable on a limited training budget, and a pure update function is easier to drop into locallm's loop than a distributed class.
caveat: The class as written asserts a list of parameters and uses torch.distributed rank sharding, so a single-GPU run needs the update function used directly or a single-device wrapper; embeddings, norms and output head must stay on Adam; the benefit is the author's claim on other tasks.
code_note: zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 asserts G.ndim >= 2 and notes it is batched; muon_update lerps the momentum buffer, optionally takes the Nesterov combination, reshapes 4-D filters, orthogonalises with ns_steps iterations and returns the update; the Muon class pads the parameter list to a multiple of the world size and has each rank update its slice.
falsifier: Compare muon_update on the 2-D hidden weights with AdamW on the same token budget; if held-out validation loss improves by under 0.02 nats, or the first-sample pass count on the 232 held-out problems stays at or below 3, it does not help.

take: canifinetune answers whether an open-weight model can be fine-tuned on one consumer NVIDIA GPU before loading weights, producing a memory breakdown, sequence length, batch size and LoRA rank suggestions and a runnable recipe, with benchmark modules that trace memory and provoke out-of-memory failures. It would pick safe LoRA settings for the RTX 4080's 16 GB.
why: Training budget is limited and a failed run on the single local card wastes a night; a preflight estimate is cheap.
caveat: Estimates are for transformers-style LoRA and QLoRA recipes, not locallm's own model class; MIT; the numbers it produces must be checked against a measured run on the 4080.
falsifier: Compare its predicted peak memory with the measured peak for 3 locallm configurations; if any prediction is off by more than 15 percent, it is not a reliable preflight.

take: Use Pynguin to generate unit tests for a problem's Python reference solution by a search that maximises coverage, and use its assertion generator, which records observed values as assertions and then filters them by mutation analysis, optionally in a fresh subprocess. The generated inputs and recorded outputs become extra examples against which a t specification is checked.
why: A specification is checked against the problem's three tests and a Python solution; a search-generated suite of inputs exercises branches those tests miss, where a weak or wrong specification could be exposed.
caveat: It executes the code under test, so it must run in a sandbox; recorded assertions encode the reference solution's behaviour, including its bugs (the MBPP 412 reference deletes from the list it iterates); the repository root carries LLM-agent instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md) that are not part of the take.
code_note: assertiongenerator.py imports a mutation-analysis controller, defines create_filtering_executor to give filtering a fresh-subprocess executor when filter_assertions_in_subprocess is set, builds an ExceptionSignature from an execution result, and its AssertionGenerator visits test-suite chromosomes to add and filter assertions so a flaky or crashing assertion is discarded instead of kept.
falsifier: Generate suites for the 232 reference solutions; if suites reach new branches or outputs for fewer than 10 percent of problems beyond the existing tests, or expose none of the 11 clean specifications as disagreeing with the reference, it adds nothing.

take: This benchmark scores LLM-written test suites on anti-fragility, rigor, mocking discipline and reuse against human baselines rather than coverage, for Python, JS/TS and Go, and ships its scorer check and ablation results as files. Its multi-axis scorecard is a template for judging whether generated checks are strong, beyond a pass rate.
why: dawnr already has a spec_scorecard; an externally validated set of quality axes is a comparison point for the axes it chooses.
caveat: The repository is packaged as a Claude Code skill and its experiment outputs come from model-written suites, so they are evidence about method only; the scripts and prompts directories were listed, not read.
falsifier: Map its axes to the existing scorecard's columns; if two or more axes have no counterpart, add them and see whether the clean specifications' ranking changes.

take: A single header defining design-by-contract macros for embedded C and C++: DBC_REQUIRE, DBC_ENSURE, DBC_INVARIANT, DBC_ERROR and DBC_ASSERT, each calling a user-supplied DBC_fault_handler with a module name and label when the expression is false. The labelled macros give a uniform way to state pre- and postconditions of a C function that CBMC treats as assertions.
why: Native cases state specifications in the harness only; contracts inside the function make the intended behaviour part of the pinned source.
caveat: Last push 2023; MIT; the fault handler must be defined, which under CBMC should be an assertion failure; modifying the pinned source defeats the purpose of extracting it unchanged.
falsifier: Express the PX4 wrap_bin contract with these macros and verify; if CBMC does not report the same counterexample as the harness assertions, the translation is not faithful.

take: Read coqtop.py for how a Python class drives Coq through its XML protocol: it finds coqtop, selects an XML interface by Coq version, starts the process, sends commands with an optional timeout, and raises CoqtopError or DuneError with the process output. It is a pure-Python driver that returns goals and error locations, unlike a single coqc call, for the Rocq lowering.
why: Rocq failures come back as a compiler exit status and text; a protocol driver gives the goal state and the failing sentence, the information repair needs.
caveat: Written for the Vim plugin, so coqtail.py depends on Vim's Python interface and only coqtop.py is a stand-alone candidate; it supports the Coq versions its xmlInterface knows, which must be checked against the Rocq release dawnr pins; MIT.
code_note: coqtop.py defines CoqtopError and DuneError, a Coqtop class holding an optional XML interface chosen from the discovered version (asserted unset before start), wraps dune failures as DuneError with decoded stderr, and its dispatch methods accept a timeout argument.
falsifier: Drive the 213 verified programs' Rocq outputs through it and record goal text for failures; if it cannot start or loses sync on more than 5 of 213, or the pinned Rocq version is unsupported, it does not help.

take: Study the corpus pipeline of a sibling project, toke, a compiled language designed for LLM code generation with a small grammar and compiler verification: a deduplicator using exact hashes plus character n-gram Jaccard similarity, a correction loop that resubmits the latest failed source with structured compiler errors up to max_attempts and escalates, an error-injection module that makes broken variants, and a differential-test voter. Each stage maps to a stage of dawnr's teacher and twin pipeline.
why: Teacher recipes added zero rows after losing replies at static checking; a project with the same architecture shows how it stages generation, validation, correction and dedup.
caveat: The repository's LICENSE is Apache-2.0 for the pipeline code, but its LICENSES.md lists third-party sources (for example CC-BY-SA-3.0 Exercism content) behind the corpus data, which is not taken; the generation and correction stages call language models, so any model-written text must follow dawnr's rule on training data; the project is new with no stars; the GitHub licence field is empty, so the licence is read from the file.
code_note: Deduplicator in dedup.py keeps a dict of exact content hashes and a dict of character n-gram sets with a configurable ngram_size and compares new items by Jaccard similarity; CorrectionLoop sends each attempt the most recent failed source with its compiler result, records a CorrectionAttempt per try and an escalated flag in CorrectionResult when attempts are exhausted, so failures end in a recorded state rather than a silent drop.
falsifier: Apply its dedup stage to the 6,954 training rows with a 0.8 Jaccard threshold; if it removes fewer than 1 percent of rows, or removes any row pair a person judges to differ in specification, near-duplicates are not the cause of zero new rows.

take: Lift the integrity design of a task's check.sh: Task.lean is split into provided and editable sections by BEGIN and END markers, a hash covers the provided sections, and the script runs the verification, stub detection, integrity check, a cheat scan of everything outside the editable parts, and an axiom audit, with modes for compile-only, integrity-only and cheats-only. It is a worked guard against an answer that weakens the statement it was meant to prove.
why: Never weakening a specification or letting a tactic chain succeed without closing its goal is a rule that has failed here before; a hashed provided-section plus cheat scan enforces it mechanically.
caveat: Bash and Lean 4 with Mathlib and Plausible imports, so it needs a lake setup per task; written for tasks with a provided statement and an editable proof, not for a lowering that generates both; the tasks are 64-bit bit-vector functions from LLVM and the eBPF verifier.
code_note: check.sh sets pipefail, extracts sections between '-- === BEGIN: NAME (provided|editable) ===' and '-- === END: NAME ===' markers, hashes only provided sections (a .provided_hash file sits in each task), carves out all text outside editable sections for the cheat scan, and accepts flags --compile, --check-integrity and --cheats-only FILE.
falsifier: Apply the section-hash and cheat-scan idea to the Lean lowering's output for the 213 programs and 213 broken twins; if it flags no weakened or stubbed statement, the lowering is already clean on this set, and if it flags any, count them.

take: clever-prover is the baseline for the CLEVER Lean benchmark, with separate evaluation entry points for generating a specification and for generating a provable implementation, few-shot baselines, a checkpoint module for resuming long runs and plots of compilation success and proof rate per stage. Splitting 'specification generation' from 'implementation generation' and reporting each stage's compile and prove rates is the accounting dawnr's funnel does by hand.
why: Where in the funnel answers are lost (compile, prove, match the specification) decides what to fix; this baseline reports compilation success and proved counts for both specification and implementation.
caveat: Needs Ray and vLLM per its init modules and a secret_template.json for API keys; five stars and a notebook-based README; Lean 4 problems from HumanEval, not t.
falsifier: Report dawnr's funnel in the same four columns (spec compiles, spec proved, impl compiles, impl proved) for the 232 problems; if the existing reports already contain all four, it adds no accounting.

take: This is the training and inference code of Huginn-0125, a depth-recurrent language model that reuses a block of layers a variable number of times, with a recpre package, a small fine-tuning example and an evaluation folder. Recurrence spends more compute per parameter, which is the direction dawnr's per-parameter question points to when a bigger model is not the limit.
why: Between 27B and 235B parameters the clean count did not move, so more depth per parameter at the same size is a candidate that parameter scaling is not.
caveat: The model was trained at scale on 4096 AMD GPUs per its README, so only the architecture and the small fine-tuning example are of interest on one RTX 4080; the technical report's claims were not checked.
falsifier: Train a recurrent-depth variant and a fixed-depth model of equal parameter count on the same tokens; if the held-out clean answers on 232 problems do not differ by 2 or more, recurrence is not the lever at this scale.

take: torchtitan is a PyTorch-native implementation that its README says takes one readable codebase from pretraining through supervised fine-tuning to reinforcement learning, with a torchtitan_recipes folder of configurations and an RL subfolder. Its single-codebase, config-driven structure is a reference for unifying locallm's pretraining, SFT and verifier-reward runs.
why: locallm's experiments (factorial, pretraining study, continue, SFT) are separate scripts; one config-driven path reduces duplicated checkpoint and data code.
caveat: Targets multi-GPU parallelism with FSDP, tensor, pipeline and expert dimensions that one card does not use; the single-device path was not inspected.
falsifier: Port one locallm run to a torchtitan-style config; if reproducing its final validation loss within 0.01 nats takes more than a day, the refactor is not worth it.

take: OmniQuant learns clipping and equivalent-transformation parameters for weight-only (W4A16, W3A16, W2A16) and weight-activation quantisation, with a quantize package and a model zoo. A learned, calibrated quantiser is the option to compare with simple round-to-nearest GGUF types for the local model.
why: Cold start and memory peak of dawnr ask depend on the quantisation level the model survives.
caveat: Outputs a quantised model in its own format, which would need conversion to GGUF; evaluations are on general language tasks.
falsifier: Quantise the locallm checkpoint to 4 bits with it and with the GGUF Q4 types; if the clean count on 232 problems differs by less than 1, the learned method is not worth the conversion.

take: Marlin is an FP16 by INT4 matmul kernel for LLM inference that its README says gives close to 4x speedup up to batch sizes of 16 to 32 and names speculative decoding and CoT-majority as use cases. Many-sample inference with a verifier choosing the winner is exactly that batch regime.
why: Answer rate may be a search budget; drawing many samples at once is cheap only if small-batch quantised matmuls are fast.
caveat: CUDA kernel written for Ampere-class GPUs (the RTX 4080 is Ada, not checked); last push 2024-09; integrates via PyTorch, not llama.cpp.
falsifier: Measure batch-16 decode throughput of the locallm model with and without it on the 4080; if the gain is under 1.5 times, drop it.

take: Lift two pieces of its harness-writing pipeline: code_fixer.py repairs frequent build errors of a generated harness with regular-expression rules (a missing member, a missing header, an unknown type) before asking a model, and fuzz_target_error.py defines a taxonomy of why a generated target fails (crash near initialisation, crash in the target, memory leak, out-of-memory, timeout, no coverage increase, null dereference, signal). The same two ideas fit drafting CBMC harnesses.
why: Every native harness is hand-written; a drafter needs deterministic repairs for the common build errors and a way to say that a failure came from the harness rather than the code under test.
caveat: Built around OSS-Fuzz projects and libFuzzer targets with model back ends from several vendors; its taxonomy is for fuzz crashes, so CBMC outcomes (unreachable goals, vacuity, unwinding failures) would be a different table; Apache-2.0; project-specific fixes in collect_specific_fixes.
code_note: code_fixer.py defines regexes for 'no member named', 'file not found' and 'unknown type name' build errors, collects project- and language-specific fix functions in collect_specific_fixes and writes fixed targets and logs into output directories; fuzz_target_error.py's SemanticCheckResult enumerates outcomes such as NO_SEMANTIC_ERR, FP_NEAR_INIT_CRASH, FP_TARGET_CRASH, FP_MEMLEAK, FP_OOM, FP_TIMEOUT, NO_COV_INCREASE, NULL_DEREF and SIGNAL, so a failure always gets a named class.
falsifier: Classify the failures of 20 model-drafted CBMC harnesses with an adapted taxonomy and fix build errors with regexes first; if the regexes repair fewer than 20 percent of the build failures, the deterministic stage does not help.

take: Lift the citation metrics of ALCE's eval.py: an NLI-based AutoAIS check (a T5 model, google/t5_xxl_true_nli_mixture, asked whether a cited passage entails a generated claim) used to compute citation recall (do the cited passages jointly support the sentence) and citation precision (is each citation needed), beside exact-match recall and ROUGE for correctness. The two-sided measure is what cite_docs lacks beyond quotation presence.
why: A citation can quote a real sentence that does not support the claim, and a claim can be supported without being cited; recall and precision measure both.
caveat: The NLI model it names is T5-XXL, too large for the laptop, so the entailment call must be swapped for a small checker such as MiniCheck; the code loads models into module globals and uses mauve and rouge dependencies not needed here; last push 2024-10.
code_note: eval.py sets AUTOAIS_MODEL, keeps the model and tokenizer in module-level globals initialised to None, _run_nli_autoais builds an entailment prompt from passage and claim, generates up to 10 tokens and decodes the result as the verdict, and compute_claims and compute_qa aggregate per-sample scores; exact_presence checks short answers in the context.
falsifier: Score the citation output of the 200 evaluation questions with recall and precision using a small entailment checker; if the two measures agree with the present quotation check on every item, they add nothing.

take: pdfplumber, built on pdfminer.six, gives every character, rectangle and line of a PDF page with coordinates and extracts tables, in pure Python. Character boxes let an extraction cite a page region and let a checker confirm that quoted text lies where the citation says.
why: Grounded extraction needs a span a reader can locate; a pure-Python coordinate extractor installs the same on Linux, macOS and Windows.
caveat: Slower than native PDF libraries and only for text-based PDFs; MIT.
falsifier: Locate 100 quoted spans by character boxes in 20 PDFs; if fewer than 95 are found at the stated page, drop it.

take: pySBD is a rule-based sentence boundary disambiguator for Python that handles abbreviations, numbers and lists, and can return character offsets of sentences. Sentence offsets define the unit a citation points to, so a quote is cited by sentence index instead of by free text.
why: Citation precision and recall are computed per sentence; a deterministic segmenter makes the unit reproducible.
caveat: Rule-based and tuned for English; last push 2024-08; legal and scientific text with unusual abbreviations may segment wrongly.
falsifier: Segment 50 pages of test documents and compare with a person's sentence marks; if more than 5 percent of boundaries differ, citation units are unreliable.

take: Owl generates parsers for visibly pushdown languages that its README says always run in linear time and whose model, like regular expressions, can be understood without talking about parser states or lookahead, with an interpreter mode for designing grammars without writing code. A grammar class with guaranteed linear-time deterministic recognition is a candidate for the prefix check inside a decoding loop.
why: A prefix-validity check runs for every generated token; linear-time parsing bounds its cost, and nested-bracket structure covers most of a spec language.
caveat: C program built with make; MIT; visibly pushdown languages require nesting to be visible in the tokens, which t's grammar may not satisfy without changes.
falsifier: Write t's grammar in Owl's notation; if it is rejected as outside the class, or the prefix check takes over 10 ms on the longest program, drop it.

take: A collection of Lark grammars (bc, GEDCOM, eqn and others) described as suitable for the lark parser and for Hypothesis, which can draw strings from a Lark grammar. The pairing shows how a grammar yields both a parser and a test-input generator, which a t grammar could do for fuzzing the front end and lowerings with valid programs.
why: The seven lowerings are tested on verified programs and their twins only; grammar-generated programs exercise forms nobody wrote.
caveat: ISC licence; last push 2024-03; grammars are for other languages and only the pairing technique is of use.
falsifier: Generate 1,000 t programs from the grammar and run the Python interpreter and one lowering; if fewer than 50 percent pass the static checker, the generator needs semantic constraints.

take: Schemathesis generates test inputs from API schemas, adapts to responses and chains operations into workflows, and keeps corpus directories of schemas. Generating cases from a declared schema and checking responses against it is the property-based pattern for checking a function against a stated signature and specification.
why: Specification checks need inputs generated from the declared types and preconditions, with failures shrunk to small cases.
caveat: Aimed at HTTP APIs (OpenAPI, GraphQL, gRPC), so only its generation and reporting design carries over; Python with Hypothesis underneath; MIT.
falsifier: Port the generate-and-check loop to 20 problems' signatures; if it finds no counterexample for known-wrong specifications within 1,000 cases, the generator is too weak.

take: SATurne is a purely functional SAT solver written and verified in Coq that, per its README, produces proofs, with proof_check.ml as a checker and Extract.v for extraction to OCaml; it is described as small, well documented and not designed for performance. A solver whose soundness is machine-checked can independently decide the tiny formulas of the native controls, so a verdict on them no longer rests on trust in a large solver.
why: The SAT solver is trusted with no proof certificate; a verified solver for small control formulas removes the trust at least where it is cheap to do so.
caveat: Not designed for performance or scale, so it covers only controls small enough to solve; last push 2022-01; needs Coq and OCaml and a formula in its input format.
falsifier: Solve the formulas of the synthetic controls with it; if it cannot finish any real native formula within 10 minutes, it covers only toy cases.

take: tt (installed from PyPI as ttable) is a Python toolkit for Boolean expressions and truth tables that parses expressions, builds truth tables and converts forms; its README says it is tested on the latest three major CPython versions. It can generate and check small CNF encodings in Python when testing a SAT back end.
why: Cross-checking a solver or a proof checker needs many small, correct formulas whose satisfiability is known by exhaustive truth table.
caveat: Truth tables grow exponentially, so it is only for formulas with a few dozen variables; MIT.
falsifier: Generate 100 random 12-variable CNFs, label them with truth tables and compare with CaDiCaL; if the solver ever disagrees with the table, one of them has a bug.

take: Harbor, from the creators of Terminal-Bench, evaluates and optimises agents and models in parallel isolated environments, lets you build and share benchmarks and environments, and keeps adapters that convert existing benchmarks and a registry.json of datasets. Its task format (instruction, environment, verifier) is the packaging that Repo2RLEnv also uses.
why: Every dawnr number links to a script; a shared task format would let others re-run the verified-answer funnel on their own models.
caveat: Targets agents running commands in containers on cloud providers; parallelism comes from remote sandboxes that dawnr does not use; the adapters directory was listed, not read.
falsifier: Write 5 dawnr problems in its task format with the seven-way gate as the verifier; if the verifier cannot return the 7-vote result in a single pass/fail, the format is too coarse.

take: EvolKit raises the complexity of fine-tuning instructions automatically with open-source language models, with run_evol.py to evolve instructions, gen_answers.py to answer them and a notebook that visualises the evolution. Applied to problem statements it is a way to produce harder variants of covered problems, whose answers the gate then keeps or discards.
why: Teacher recipes lose replies on easy repeated problems; harder variants of verified problems are a controlled expansion whose labels still come from the gate.
caveat: The generation models must be ones whose output dawnr may train on (not the excluded families); last push 2024-10; evolved instructions may drift from a problem the reference tests can check.
falsifier: Evolve 50 solved problems one step and run the teacher on them; if fewer than 5 yield a new clean problem, evolution is not an expansion path.

take: mpmath is a pure-Python library for arbitrary-precision floating-point arithmetic. Evaluating a flight function in mpmath at 200 bits gives a reference close to the real-number result, against which the binary32 and binary64 evaluations can be measured, so the size of each precision's error is a number and not an assumption.
why: Flight checks use binary64 where production uses binary32; without a real-number reference the difference between them cannot be attributed.
caveat: Pure Python and slow for large sweeps; correctly rounded elementary functions in the library may differ in the last bit from the target's libm, so it is a reference for error size, not for bit equality.
falsifier: Evaluate 3 flight functions in binary32, binary64 and mpmath on 10,000 inputs; if binary32's maximum relative error to the mpmath value is under 1e-6 for every function, the binary32 gap is small in this sample.

take: Paperproof inspects how hypotheses and goals change through a Lean 4 proof and exposes that history, with Lean-side services (Paperproof.lean, BetterParser.lean, GetTheorems.lean) that produce the data for its viewer. The goal-state history of a failed Lean proof is the structured feedback a repair step needs, instead of an error message.
why: The repair rounds feed error text; per-tactic goal states show where a proof diverged.
caveat: The Lean code depends on the toolchain pinned in its lean-toolchain file and on Lean internals that change between releases; the rest is a TypeScript editor extension and a web app.
falsifier: Extract the goal history for 20 failing Lean proofs of the lowering; if fewer than 15 can be extracted, the Lean-side service is not reliable for dawnr's toolchain.

take: ugrep is a grep replacement with Boolean AND, OR and NOT queries, fuzzy search, a query TUI and search inside archives, compressed files and PDFs, with an msvc directory beside the autotools build. It could back the assistant's text-search tool with ranked fuzzy and Boolean queries across all three platforms.
why: A small model asks for imprecise searches; fuzzy and Boolean matching tolerate that better than exact regular expressions.
caveat: C++ binary installed separately (BSD-3-Clause); the Windows build is through the msvc and vs directories; output format differs from ripgrep, which a tool wrapper must parse.
falsifier: Replay 100 recorded assistant searches with fuzzy matching on; if fewer than 10 more find the intended file than with exact search, drop it.

take: Chonkie is a lightweight ingestion library with several chunkers, integrations and a benchmarks document, installable from PyPI. It is a ready set of chunking strategies to compare against fixed windows for the local retrieval index, with timing figures from its own benchmarks.
why: Chunk boundaries decide retrieval quality, and trying several strategies on the repository corpus is an inexpensive experiment.
caveat: General-text oriented; whether any chunker wraps a syntax parser for code was not checked; the project also has a BENCHMARKS.md whose timing figures are its own.
falsifier: Compare 3 of its chunkers with fixed windows on recall at 10 over the retrieval set; if none beats windows by 2 points, drop it.

take: Goblint is an abstract-interpretation static analysis framework for C written in OCaml with a tests directory of regression programs and configuration files in conf. Its value ranges and loop information can propose the bounds and assumptions for a CBMC harness, to be checked by CBMC, instead of choosing unwinding bounds and input ranges by hand.
why: Loops are bounded by hand and a bound hides defects past it; a sound analyzer can state a bound that is then validated.
caveat: Built from source with opam on Linux (the README lists Linux steps first) and a Dockerfile; Windows support not confirmed; its results are over-approximations, so a proposed bound is a hypothesis for CBMC to check, not a proof of the harness.
falsifier: Ask it for loop bounds on 5 existing cases and use them as unwind limits; if CBMC 6.11 then fails an unwinding assertion in more than 1 of 5, the proposed bounds are unreliable.

take: SOAP explores optimisations of a numerical C program so that its FPGA implementation minimises error, area and latency, in Python 3 with an isabelle directory of proofs. The search over semantically equivalent rewrites of floating-point expressions, scored by an error bound, is a model for judging whether two floating-point forms of a flight function differ.
why: Flight checks compare binary32 and binary64 forms of one function; a tool that scores rewrites by error bound shows how to compare forms symbolically.
caveat: README says the tool is in an early stage and last push is 2016-05; research prototype with its own input language.
falsifier: Run it on one flight expression and compare its error bound with the sampled maximum error; if the bound is over 100 times larger, it is too loose.

take: PREVAIL is a polynomial-runtime eBPF verifier built on an abstract interpretation layer in C++, with a test-data directory and an ebpf-samples submodule of programs. Its numeric abstract domains for integer ranges show how to get sound range facts over machine integers without a solver call.
why: Cheap range pre-filters can show that an assertion cannot fail before CBMC runs, shortening easy cases.
caveat: Built for eBPF bytecode rather than C source; MIT with an additional Apache-2.0 licence file in the tree; submodules are required to build.
falsifier: Read its numeric domain interface and apply the idea to 10 scalar cases; if fewer than 3 are settled without CBMC, the pre-filter saves little.

take: This pipeline uses one 7B open-source model (Qwen2.5-Coder) on vLLM to find, prove and patch C memory-safety bugs, with AddressSanitizer as the ground-truth oracle: a bug counts as proved by re-detonation and a patch must pass a build, a proof-of-concept stop, a regression run and a re-attack ladder. It is the same shape as dawnr's loop (model proposal, sanitizer replay, gate) at the scale of one local GPU.
why: Finding-to-case cost is the bottleneck on real bugs and the local model is small; this shows a published loop where a small model proposes and a sanitizer, not the model, decides.
caveat: The README's result is for a canary target with 3 planted bugs, which says little about real projects; 18 stars and one author; its numbers are its own; notebook plus scripts layout.
falsifier: Run its patch-validation ladder on 5 of dawnr's fixed defects with the original replay inputs; if it accepts a patch that still fails replay under UBSan, the ladder is weaker than the gate.

take: LibRedFat is a hardened malloc and free built on poisoned redzones and low-fat pointers, used with LD_PRELOAD or by static linking without recompiling the target. Preloading it under the native replay adds a second memory-error detector for a binary that was built without AddressSanitizer.
why: Replay compiles with ASan and UBSan by hand; a preloadable allocator adds heap-bound checking for prebuilt binaries and a different detector for the same witness.
caveat: Its usage is through LD_PRELOAD, a Unix mechanism, so Windows needs static linking or another route; last push 2023-09; which error classes it covers beyond heap was not checked.
falsifier: Preload it for the replay of 3 heap-related witnesses; if it reports none that ASan did not, it adds no detection.

take: Lift the guardrail state machine for tool-calling with a small local model: a check on each response returns one of execute, retry, tool_error, step_blocked or fatal, a bad response triggers a corrective nudge message up to max_retries consecutive times, tool-call text is rescued from plain prose when rescue_enabled, and premature terminal calls are counted separately. It fits dawnr_agent's loop around the local model and llama-server.
why: A small model's tool calls fail on format more than on judgement, which is the assistant-side form of the parse wall; a bounded retry-and-rescue layer is a measured remedy in the project's own suite.
caveat: The README's figures (an 8B local model from single digits to 84 percent on its 26-scenario suite) are the project's own and were not reproduced; it ships clients for Ollama, vLLM, Anthropic, llamafile and OpenAI-compatible servers, of which only llama-server matters; it has install.sh and install.ps1 for Linux, macOS and Windows.
code_note: guardrails.py defines CheckResult with an action literal (execute, retry, tool_error, step_blocked, fatal), the tool calls to run, and a nudge message to inject on retry; Guardrails.__init__ takes max_retries=3 for consecutive bad responses, max_tool_errors=2, rescue_enabled=True, max_premature_attempts=3 and an optional retry_nudge callable, so every failure mode has a cap and ends in a named action instead of a loop.
falsifier: Run the local model through 100 recorded assistant tool-call tasks with and without such guardrails; if the share completing correctly does not rise by 10 points, or the extra retries raise median latency by more than 2 times, it does not help.

take: kvpress implements several KV-cache compression methods and a benchmark harness on top of Hugging Face transformers, installable with pip install kvpress. For long repository contexts on the 16 GB card, compressing the cache is an alternative to retrieving less.
why: Context management for the repository assistant is limited by KV-cache memory on the laptop as much as by the window length.
caveat: Works with transformers models, not through llama.cpp, whose own cache quantisation is the deployable route; the README's motivating figures are for 70B models.
falsifier: Compress the cache of the local model at 50 percent on 30 long-context questions; if answer correctness falls by more than 2 answers of 30, compression costs too much.

take: Mixture-of-Recursions (NeurIPS 2025) learns a dynamic number of recursive layer applications per token, with a model package, a pretrain.py script and configuration directories. It is a second route, beside Huginn's fixed recurrence, to spend compute per token without adding parameters, tested with a pretraining script small enough to read.
why: The 27B and 235B models gave the same clean count, so compute per parameter, not size, is the open variable; per-token adaptive depth lets easy tokens exit early.
caveat: Pretraining configs use DeepSpeed (ds_configs) and FineWeb, so a single-card run needs a reduced config; Apache-2.0; claims are the paper's.
falsifier: Pretrain a small recursion model and a plain model at equal parameters on the t-source corpus; if validation loss differs by under 0.02 nats, adaptive depth does not help at this scale.

take: The K Framework lets a language be defined once as a K specification and compiled to an interpreter, a model checker and a deductive verifier, with a Python API (pyk), a Haskell symbolic backend and an LLVM backend. That is the opposite design to writing seven separate lowerings: one executable semantics of t whose proofs share a single definition.
why: Seven lowerings that each re-implement t's semantics can agree or disagree for reasons of translation; a single semantics from which verifiers are derived shows what the translation gap is.
caveat: Heavy toolchain (Nix install per its README, Java, Haskell and LLVM backends); the K definition of t would be a new artefact; BSD-3-Clause for the framework.
falsifier: Write the K semantics of 5 t programs and compare its symbolic verdicts with the Dafny and Lean lowerings; if K disagrees with either on any of the 5, a lowering has a semantic gap.

take: CertiRocq compiles Gallina, the specification language of the Rocq Prover, to WebAssembly or Clight, a subset of C, with large parts of the compiler verified. Compiling the Rocq lowering of a t program to C gives a native function whose behaviour follows the proved definition, which CBMC and the sanitizer replay can then check against the original.
why: A proof in Rocq says nothing about compiled code; compiling the proved definition to C and checking that C natively closes the loop between the proof backends and the native gate.
caveat: Large OCaml and Rocq build (opam and a configure script) tied to specific Rocq versions; the README says other parts are still being verified; runtime directory supplies the C runtime that the generated code needs and would enlarge the CBMC model.
falsifier: Compile 5 Rocq-lowered programs to Clight and run them natively on 1,000 inputs; if any output differs from the Python interpreter, either the lowering or the compiler path has a gap.

take: nearley is an Earley parsing toolkit for JavaScript with a grammar description language and a parser that its README calls streaming, fed text incrementally, and a lib directory holding the parser and grammar compiler. Its small streaming Earley core (columns of states advanced per character) is a readable reference for an incremental prefix-validity check on t.
why: An incremental Earley recognizer decides at each token whether a prefix can still be completed, which is the check constrained decoding needs.
caveat: JavaScript, last push 2024-11; it must be ported to Python; ambiguity handling returns several parses, which a prefix check does not need.
falsifier: Port the recognizer core and measure per-token time on the longest t program; if it exceeds 5 ms, it is too slow for a decoding loop.

take: Camelot extracts tables from PDFs with five parsers: lattice for ruled tables, stream for whitespace, network and hybrid based on text alignment, and an optional neural parser for borderless tables, with a flavor setting that picks one automatically. Numbers in tables are the values extraction must get exactly right and cite.
why: Grounded extraction of numbers from financial or legal tables fails first at table structure, not at the model.
caveat: Python with optional ghostscript or image dependencies for some parsers and a neural option that adds a large model; text-based PDFs only for most flavors.
falsifier: Extract 50 tables from 10 test PDFs and compare cell values with a hand copy; if more than 3 percent of numeric cells differ, drop it.

take: Defects4J is a database of 854 reproducible bugs from open-source Java projects with an infrastructure in framework that checks out the buggy and fixed versions and runs the tests of each. The fail-on-buggy, pass-on-fixed protocol per bug is the benchmark design to copy when turning native findings and their fixes into a repair test set.
why: A repair test set needs reproducible buggy and fixed pairs with tests that separate them, the same discipline as dawnr's twins.
caveat: Java projects only and a Perl-based command-line framework; MIT; the bugs themselves are fetched from the project repositories.
falsifier: Describe 20 native findings in its record style (project, buggy commit, fixed commit, tests); if fewer than 10 have a fixed commit and a separating test, the set is too small to serve as a repair benchmark.

take: kGenProg reimplements GenProg, a genetic-algorithm repair system for Java that mutates code until the failing tests pass, requiring JDK 11 or later and shipping a jar. Search-based repair that uses only the tests as feedback is a model-free baseline to compare with model-written repairs under the same test budget.
why: Answer rate may be a search budget; a mutation search over candidate repairs is the other way to spend one.
caveat: Java for Java programs; the test-driven fitness cannot fix specifications without a test that fails on them.
falsifier: Apply the genetic search idea with the gate's mutants as operators to 20 failing cells; if it repairs fewer than the model-written round (3 of 182 cells), drop it.

take: AQLM compresses language models by additive quantization with learned codebooks and PV-Tuning, with a conversion script to the Hugging Face format and an inference_lib; its README reports 1-bit models of Llama-2-7B. It is the aggressive end of the compression range to try if the local model must fit a small memory budget.
why: Cold start and the 6.8 GB peak are costs of dawnr ask; the lowest bit width a code model survives sets the floor.
caveat: Needs its own inference kernels, not llama.cpp; compression itself requires calibration data and a GPU for hours per model; the accuracy figures in the README are for general language benchmarks.
falsifier: Compress a 7B code model to 2 bits and check pass rate on 232 problems; if it falls by more than 30 percent of the full-precision count, extreme compression is unsafe for code.

take: Pydantic turns Python type hints into validators and JSON schemas, with json_schema.py generating the schema and type_adapter.py applying it to arbitrary types. A problem's signature, written as type hints, can be turned into the JSON schema that restricts types for the Cohere structured-output path or a llama.cpp grammar, and the same models validate the reply.
why: The next teacher trial builds schemas from the problem's signature that restrict types; pydantic produces schema and validation from one definition.
caveat: Cohere omits some schema features (minItems, maxItems, allOf, oneOf), so generated schemas must be filtered through a capability probe; pydantic's schemas use constructs such as anyOf and references that must be checked against the same list; Python 3.10 or later.
falsifier: Generate schemas for the 50 frozen uncovered problems' signatures and run the capability probe; if more than 10 of 50 use unsupported keywords, a rewriting step is needed before any trial.

take: FastMCP builds Model Context Protocol servers and clients from ordinary Python, where a decorator on a typed function with a docstring becomes a tool whose input schema comes from the type hints. It would expose dawnr's harness tools (file read, search, calculator) to any MCP client with a few lines per tool, and a fastmcp_slim directory is listed at the root (its contents were not read).
why: dawnr_harness already has an MCP server module; a maintained framework removes the protocol handling and gives schemas from signatures.
caveat: Large dependency set; the slim variant's contents were not read; the project also ships remote and tasks packages that dawnr does not need.
falsifier: Re-implement the existing MCP tools with it; if the tool schemas it emits differ from the current ones in required fields for more than 2 tools, a compatibility layer is needed.

take: The official Python SDK implements the Model Context Protocol for servers and clients and keeps a schema directory beside its sources and examples. It is the reference to test dawnr_harness's own mcp_client.py and mcp_server.py against for protocol conformance.
why: Handwritten protocol code drifts from the specification; talking to the reference implementation shows where.
caveat: Adds a dependency tree (pydantic, an async stack); the SDK's version moves with the protocol version, which must be pinned.
falsifier: Run dawnr's MCP server against the SDK client on its tool list and call paths; if any request fails, the hand-written server is out of spec.

take: tree-splicer parses input files with tree-sitter grammars and generates new test cases by splicing their syntax trees, and its README notes that tree-sitter grammars are resistant to syntax errors. Splicing subtrees of verified t programs gives new programs for differential tests of the seven lowerings without writing a generator.
why: Seven lowerings are tested on verified programs and twins only; spliced variants reach combinations nobody wrote.
caveat: Rust crate needing a tree-sitter grammar for t, which does not exist and would have to be written; spliced programs are not guaranteed to type-check or terminate.
falsifier: Splice 500 variants of the 213 programs and run the interpreter and Dafny lowering; if every variant that passes the static check agrees between the two, the lowerings are consistent on this family.

take: Domato generates test inputs from a grammar written in its own rule format, with generator.py and grammar.py implementing the expansion and a rules directory of grammars for several languages. A small generator that expands weighted rules with variable definitions is a lightweight alternative to a parser-based mask when sampling syntactically valid programs.
why: Sampling from a grammar produces valid programs by construction, a baseline for how many valid t programs a model-free generator yields.
caveat: Apache-2.0 research tool for DOM fuzzing; its rule format has no semantic constraints, so generated programs still need the static checker.
falsifier: Write t's grammar in its rule format and sample 1,000 programs; if fewer than 30 percent pass the static check, grammar sampling alone is not a usable baseline.

take: Fuzzinator is a Python framework that runs fuzzers and test-generating tools, collects the issues they find, and manages them through a pipeline, installable from PyPI, with examples of configuration. The orchestration of generate, detect, deduplicate and report is the missing layer between a model finding and a filed case.
why: The finding-to-case cost is the bottleneck; a framework that dedups and tracks issues across runs turns many sanitizer hits into a short list.
caveat: BSD-3-Clause; configuration-driven and tied to its own plugin model; only its issue-handling concepts are needed.
falsifier: Feed it the sanitizer failures of 50 fuzzing runs on one pinned project; if it merges fewer than 30 percent of duplicates, the dedup is too weak.

take: Ragas defines evaluation metrics for retrieval-augmented applications as separate modules, among them faithfulness, context precision, context recall, answer correctness and factual correctness. The split of 'is the answer supported by the context' from 'did retrieval return what was needed' is the decomposition to apply when judging dawnr ask answers.
why: dawnr_retrieval is judged by recall alone; a wrong answer can come from retrieval or from reading, and separate metrics tell which.
caveat: Most metrics call a language model as judge, so the judge must be a model dawnr may use and its labels are not training data; large dependency tree; the Python 3.12 install was not checked.
falsifier: Score 100 assistant answers with faithfulness and context recall against hand labels; if either metric agrees with the labels less than 80 percent of the time using a local judge, it is not usable.

take: The Hugging Face tokenizers library trains and applies tokenizers (BPE, WordPiece and others) in Rust with Python bindings and serialises them to one JSON file. Training a vocabulary on t source and C with it, then converting for llama.cpp, is the route to testing a code-specific tokenizer without writing one.
why: A tokenizer has silently eaten text in this project; a widely used implementation with offset mapping makes loss visible.
caveat: Its README says the library is moving from 0.23 to a v1.0.0 release candidate that does not ship all features yet; wheels are prebuilt for common platforms but Python 3.12 or later must be checked.
falsifier: Train an 8k vocabulary on the t corpus and compare tokens per program and decode round trips on all training files; if any file fails to round-trip, the tokenizer is not safe.

take: tiktoken is a fast byte-pair tokeniser whose README example asserts that decoding the encoding of a string returns the string, with a Rust core, Python package and tests directory. The round-trip assertion is a one-line integrity check that can be run over every training file for any tokenizer.
why: Silent text loss in tokenizers has already cost a run; a standard round-trip assertion over the whole corpus is cheap.
caveat: The encodings it ships are OpenAI's; for dawnr's own vocabulary only the method and its tests are of use; MIT.
falsifier: Run decode(encode(text)) == text over the 6,954 training rows with each tokenizer in use; if any row fails, the tokenizer loses text.

take: llama.vim is a Vim plugin for local fill-in-the-middle completion against a llama.cpp server, with a ring context of chunks from open and edited files and yanked text, a limit on maximum generation time, a configurable scope of context around the cursor and instruction-based editing. The ring-context design is a ready answer to what extra context a small FIM model should see.
why: The assistant's local model completes code on a small context budget; this plugin shows a tested policy for filling it from the editing session.
caveat: Vimscript client for llama-server; only the context-selection policy and time limit transfer; MIT.
falsifier: Replay 50 edit positions with a ring context from recent files versus the enclosing function only; if exact-match completion does not rise by 5 points, the ring adds nothing.

take: llama2.c trains a small Llama-architecture model in PyTorch and runs it with a 700-line C file (run.c), with export.py writing the model to a flat binary, runq.c for quantised inference, test_all.py, and Windows support files (win.c, win.h, build_msvc.bat). It is a full small-model train-export-infer stack that compiles on all three platforms with no dependencies.
why: Cold start of 64.6 s and 6.8 GB peak are properties of the runtime; a 700-line baseline shows the floor for a model of locallm's size.
caveat: Last push 2024-08; supports the Llama 2 architecture only, so locallm must match it; its tokenizer is its own binary format.
falsifier: Export a locallm-size checkpoint to its format and time cold start and peak memory against llama.cpp; if llama.cpp is not slower, the baseline gives no new information.
